- **Denominations and record series confirmed by tool results:**
  - **Dutch Reformed Church** — The oldest continuous registration series in the city, beginning 1639 and running through the colonial period and beyond. FamilySearch has digitized 1 volume covering Dutch Reformed Church registers for New York City, 1700–1776 (imageGroupNumber 007733180; 211 images). **Access level: browse-only images** — `recordSearchablePercent` is 0 and `fulltextSearchable` is false. **Critical note: this volume is in Dutch.** You must be able to read 18th-century Dutch script to use it, or use a translator.
  - **Anglican / Trinity Church** — Trinity Church (founded 1696) kept baptism, marriage, and burial registers. The wiki_search results confirm these exist; physical originals are held by Trinity Church Archives, New York City. FamilySearch has microfilmed some Trinity registers.
  - **Presbyterian, French Reformed (Huguenot), Lutheran** — All kept registers. The wiki_search results name the New-York Historical Society and New York Genealogical & Biographical Society as holding colonial church collections.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Church Records, 1640–1940" (collection 1469062) covers the colonial period. It contains 2,345,678 records and 1,172,839 images statewide.
- **Language:** Dutch Reformed records are in Dutch. Anglican records are in English. French Reformed records may be in French.
- **Where held:** Parish originals at each church; microfilm at the FamilySearch Library and the New York Genealogical & Biographical Society; some digitized on FamilySearch.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The first federal census was taken in 1790, at the very end of this period. It lists heads of household only (not names of all family members). It is indexed and online at Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Colonial-era enumerations:** No federal census existed before 1790. New York Province conducted occasional head-counts for tax and militia purposes, but these were not comprehensive name-by-name enumerations. Tax assessment lists and militia rolls (see below) serve as the nearest substitutes.
- **No state census** was taken during the 1700s that serves the same function as a federal census.

### Probate and court records

- **Probate:** During the colonial period, wills were proved before the **Prerogative Court of New York** (a provincial body). The wiki_search results specifically confirm that wills proved before this court are indexed in the *Abstracts of Wills* series published by the New-York Historical Society — a critical finding aid for the entire century.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971" (collection 1542780) covers the full colonial period. 987,654 records; 493,827 images statewide.
- **Court records:** The Mayor's Court of New York City heard civil matters. The wiki_search results confirm Mayor's Court records survive and are held at the New York City Municipal Archives and the New York State Archives. Naturalizations before 1906 could be filed in any court of record; the Supreme Court of New York (colonial) also heard them.
- **Access:** The FamilySearch probate collection spans the period; digitization and indexing levels within it vary by record series.

### Land records

- **System:** Metes and bounds (colonial New York used the English system after 1664). Earlier Dutch-era land grants used Dutch conventions.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Crown (via the Governor of New York Province) granted land patents during the colonial period. The New York State Archives in Albany holds colonial land patent records. After 1777, the State of New York held this authority.
- **Types:** Deeds, land patents/grants, mortgages, tax lists.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Land Records, 1630–1975" (collection 2078654). 1,567,890 records; 783,945 images. Covers the colonial period.
- **Colonial manuscripts:** The wiki_search results confirm the **New York Colonial Manuscripts** at the New York State Archives contain land conveyances and grants for the 1700s.
- **Where held:** Deeds recorded at the county level (New York County Clerk's office, now at the New York City Department of Finance); colonial patents at the New York State Archives, Albany.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702–1713), King George's War (1744–1748), French and Indian War (1754–1763), American Revolutionary War (1775–1783).
- **Record types:** Provincial militia rolls listing men of military age (the wiki_search results confirm these survive for colonial New York and name residents ward by ward); Continental Army and New York state militia service records for the Revolution.
- **Revolutionary War:** NARA holds federal-level service and pension records (accessible via Fold3 and Ancestry). The New York State Archives holds state militia records. Fold3 (fold3.com) was returned by the external links search as a curated resource.
- **Access:** Some militia lists are published in printed abstracts; NARA pension files are microfilmed and partially digitized.

### Cemetery records

- **Major colonial cemeteries in Manhattan:** Trinity Church burial ground (Broadway at Wall Street), Marble Cemetery and New York City Marble Cemetery (both early 19th century, just outside this period), Dutch Reformed churchyards, the African Burial Ground (rediscovered 1991; documented thousands of burials, 1690s–1790s).
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) was returned as a curated external resource for this place. Trinity Church burial records are partially transcribed and available through the church and the New-York Historical Society.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for colonial church burial grounds are held by the individual churches and, for some, the New-York Historical Society.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The *New-York Gazette* (founded 1725, the city's first newspaper) is the most significant colonial paper. The *New-York Weekly Journal* (1733) and others followed. They carried marriage notices, death notices, legal notices, and runaway-slave advertisements.
- **Where held:** The New York Public Library holds extensive colonial newspaper microfilm. Newspapers.com (returned as a curated external link) has some coverage; check also Readex's America's Historical Newspapers database (available through many public libraries).
- **Content value:** Obituaries and marriage notices often provide family information not found anywhere else for this period.

### Immigration / emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** New York Harbor was the primary port of entry. Passengers arriving in colonial New York were not systematically recorded at the federal level (no federal passenger list law existed until 1819).
- **Colonial arrivals:** The New York State Archives holds some colonial-era ship arrival records and lists of settlers. The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society has published transcriptions of early arrival lists.
- **Naturalizations:** Before 1906, naturalizations could be filed in any court. The Mayor's Court and Supreme Court of New York both heard them. Some colonial naturalization records are in the *New York Colonial Manuscripts*.
- **Note on passenger lists:** The federal passenger-list series (Customs lists) begins 1820 — well after this period. For the 1700s, look to published transcriptions of ship lists and colonial government records rather than federal manifests.
- **Alien registrations / declarations of intention:** Not systematically collected in the colonial period, but some are embedded in court minutes.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Provincial and city tax assessments listing taxable property by ward. The wiki_search results confirm these survive for some years and wards.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804" (collection 1678432) covers the very end of this period; 123,456 records; 61,728 images. Earlier colonial tax lists exist but are not confirmed in a named FamilySearch indexed collection from this session's tool results.
- **Substitute value:** For years between enumerations and before the 1790 census, ward tax lists can place a person at a specific address and establish property ownership.
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (colonial provincial tax records); New York City Municipal Archives (city ward assessments).

### Other record types

- **Slave records:** The African Burial Ground (1690s–1790s) and the 1712 and 1741 slave conspiracy trials generated court records naming enslaved individuals. These are at the New York State Archives and have been partially transcribed and published.
- **Indenture and apprenticeship records:** The city kept records of apprenticeships; some are held at the New York City Municipal Archives.
- **Jewish records:** Congregation Shearith Israel (founded 1654, the oldest Jewish congregation in North America) kept circumcision, marriage, and burial records. Originals are at the congregation; some are transcribed in published form.
- **Huguenot records:** The French Reformed (Huguenot) church kept registers in French; some are published by the Huguenot Society of America.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | New York, Church Records, 1640–1940 (coll. 1469062); New York, Land Records, 1630–1975 (coll. 2078654); New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971 (coll. 1542780); New York, Tax Assessment Rolls, 1799–1804 (coll. 1678432); Dutch Reformed Church Registers NYC 1700–1776 (vol. 007733180, browse-only, Dutch) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (1790 is the relevant census for this period); some NY church and court transcriptions | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War service records, pension files, colonial militia | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including some colonial NYC titles | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery inscriptions including Trinity Church burial ground | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal-level Revolutionary War and early republic records | Free (some via subscription partners) |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` at the city level returned 1 digitized volume (totalResults: 1) — the Dutch Reformed Church registers, 1700–1776, browse-only and in Dutch. The state-level `volume_search` was not separately paginated in this session. The 5 FamilySearch collections returned by `collections_search` at the state scope are the complete set returned (totalForPlace: 5); no nextPageToken was present.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New York State Archives, Albany | Colonial Manuscripts; provincial court, land, tax, and militia records; Prerogative Court of Wills | In-person; some guides at nysarches.gov |
| New York City Municipal Archives | City ward tax lists, Mayor's Court records, indentures | In-person / written request |
| New-York Historical Society | Colonial church record transcriptions; *Abstracts of Wills* series; manuscript collections | In-person; some digitized |
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS) | Colonial church records; published transcriptions; finding aids | Membership; in-person |
| Trinity Church Archives | Trinity Church baptism, marriage, burial registers from 1696 | By appointment |
| Congregation Shearith Israel | Jewish community registers from 1654 | Contact congregation |
| New York Public Library | Colonial newspaper microfilm; local history collections | In-person; some digitized |

## Records NOT online

- Most pre-1790 ward-level tax assessment lists
- Mayor's Court civil and criminal case files (physical at NYC Municipal Archives)
- Trinity Church burial and vestry records prior to any microfilming project
- Congregation Shearith Israel registers
- Huguenot church registers (partially published in print, not fully digitized)
- Lutheran church registers for the colonial period
- Most colonial provincial government records (New York Colonial Manuscripts at the State Archives — not fully digitized)
- Indenture and apprenticeship records at the NYC Municipal Archives

## Known record losses

- The **Great Fire of 1776** during the British occupation destroyed a significant portion of lower Manhattan, including structures that may have held records.
- **British military occupation (1776–1783)** disrupted normal record-keeping; some city records from this period are incomplete or missing.
- No known courthouse fire of the type that destroyed county courthouses in other states, but the fragmented custody of colonial records (split between the State Archives, the city, and private institutions) creates effective gaps.

## Research tips

- **Church records are your vital records.** Civil registration did not exist in 18th-century New York. Every birth, marriage, and death you seek was recorded — if at all — in a church register. Identify the denomination first, then find the specific congregation.
- **The Dutch Reformed registers are browse-only and in Dutch.** The single digitized FamilySearch volume (007733180, 1700–1776) cannot be name-searched. You must browse all 211 images, and you must read 18th-century Dutch. Consider engaging a professional translator or using the published transcriptions at the New-York Historical Society.
- **Wills in the *Abstracts of Wills* series.** The New-York Historical Society published multi-volume abstracts of all wills proved before the Prerogative Court of New York through the colonial period. This is the most efficient finding aid for probate research before 1800 and is available at major genealogical libraries.
- **The 1790 federal census is your only name-indexed census for this period** — and it lists only heads of household. For the rest of the century, substitute tax lists, militia rolls, and church registers.
- **Search by ward.** Colonial Manhattan was divided into wards (East Ward, West Ward, Dock Ward, etc.). Tax lists, court records, and militia rolls are often organized by ward, not alphabetically. Knowing which ward your ancestor lived in is a prerequisite for efficient searching.
- **The New York Colonial Manuscripts** at the New York State Archives are a large, partially calendared collection covering the entire provincial period. The *Calendar of Historical Manuscripts in the Office of the Secretary of State* (published in the 19th century) provides an index and is available at research libraries.
- **Check both Dutch and English name forms.** Families with Dutch origins often appear under anglicized names in English records and Dutch names in church registers. Adriaen becomes Adrian or Andrew; Hendrick becomes Henry; Van der Berg may become Vandenberg. Search both.
- **Neighboring jurisdictions matter.** A family on the east side of Manhattan's boundary may have generated records in Kings County (Brooklyn) across the East River, or Westchester County to the north. The 1790 census and church records on both sides of these borders are worth checking.
- **The wiki_search result** (source: [New York City Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)) identifies the New York Genealogical & Biographical Society and the New-York Historical Society as the two most important institutional repositories for colonial NYC research — confirm membership or access arrangements before visiting.

---

This project is focused on Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1845–1908), so a note: the New York City colonial (1700s) guide above covers a different place and century from the active research objective. If you are tracing Flynn family origins back through New York City in the colonial period, this guide applies; if the NYC connection was exploratory, the two research threads are separate.

---

New York City in the 1700s was under British colonial rule for most of the century, and no government required civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths — so the records that matter most for tracing families are church registers (especially the Dutch Reformed and Anglican / Trinity Church series), wills proved before the colonial Prerogative Court, ward-level tax lists, and provincial land patents. The most important physical repositories are the New York State Archives in Albany, the New-York Historical Society, and the New York City Municipal Archives; FamilySearch has one digitized but browse-only volume of Dutch Reformed registers in Dutch, plus broader statewide collections for church, land, and probate records.

The best next step is to identify which church denomination and which ward of Manhattan your ancestor's family belonged to — those two facts will point you to the specific register series and physical repository to consult first.

output.text_response:
Here is the locality guide's response:

---

Virginia during the Revolutionary War (1775–1783) is one of the better-documented colonial jurisdictions in America, with records kept at the county level going back to the 1630s. The most useful records for tracing families connected to military service are:

- **Pension and Bounty-Land Warrant Files** — National Archives (NARA). These are the richest source, especially widows' applications, which often include biographical detail about the soldier and family.
- **Continental Line Service Records and Muster Rolls** — also at NARA, and searchable on Fold3.
- **Virginia Militia Records** — held at the Library of Virginia in Richmond, with some digitized on FamilySearch.
- **1782–1783 Personal Property and Land Tax Lists** — these serve as the only practical substitute for Virginia's 1790 census, which was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814.

**Key things to watch for:**
- Virginia was rapidly creating new counties from older ones during this period, so the county name in a record may differ from modern boundaries.
- Kentucky was still part of Virginia until 1792 — families there appear in Virginia records.
- There were no civil birth, marriage, or death registrations at all. Church vestry registers and county court marriage bonds are the only vital record substitutes.

Several of these collections are indexed and searchable at FamilySearch and Fold3.

The next step is building a focused research plan for the specific individual or family you are tracing, using this survey as the foundation.

quirks: Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814 — substitute with the 1782-1783 personal property and land tax lists (FamilySearch collection 1456723).
Kentucky was part of Virginia until 1792 — families in present-day Kentucky during 1775-1783 appear in Virginia Land Office records and Virginia county court records.

Virginia created new counties rapidly in the 1770s-1780s; always verify which county held authority at the exact event date before searching, as the county of residence may differ from modern boundaries.
No statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed during this period — Anglican vestry registers and county court marriage bonds are the primary vital record substitutes.
Virginia land bounty warrants (FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 005301447) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only image by image.

Virginia's bounty land for Continental Line veterans was granted in the Virginia Military District of Ohio; warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia connect the Virginia soldier to the Ohio land.

Loyalist families will not appear in Virginia pension or militia records — search the Loyalist Claims Commission records at The National Archives (UK) and Virginia attainder/confiscation proceedings at the Library of Virginia.

Anglican vestry records are especially valuable because vestry minutes recorded poor-relief payments, binding of orphaned children as apprentices, and levy assessments naming all householders — many of whom appear in no other record series.

The wiki_place_page tool returned only generic content for all four Virginia wiki sections; consulting the FamilySearch Wiki for Virginia Military Records directly (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records) is strongly recommended.

Kentucky was part of Virginia until 1792 — families in present-day Kentucky during 1775-1783 appear in Virginia Land Office records and Virginia county court records.

Virginia created new counties rapidly in the 1770s-1780s; always verify which county held authority at the exact event date before searching, as the county of residence may differ from modern boundaries.
No statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed during this period — Anglican vestry registers and county court marriage bonds are the primary vital record substitutes.
Virginia land bounty warrants (FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 005301447) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only image by image.

Virginia's bounty land for Continental Line veterans was granted in the Virginia Military District of Ohio; warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia connect the Virginia soldier to the Ohio land.

Loyalist families will not appear in Virginia pension or militia records — search the Loyalist Claims Commission records at The National Archives (UK) and Virginia attainder/confiscation proceedings at the Library of Virginia.

Anglican vestry records are especially valuable because vestry minutes recorded poor-relief payments, binding of orphaned children as apprentices, and levy assessments naming all householders — many of whom appear in no other record series.

The wiki_place_page tool returned only generic content for all four Virginia wiki sections; consulting the FamilySearch Wiki for Virginia Military Records directly (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records) is strongly recommended.

Here is the locality guide's full response on New Orleans early 1800s records, disasters, and substitutes:

---

## New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana — Early 1800s Record Survival

### The disaster picture

**Two major fires — 1788 and 1794** — destroyed hundreds of structures in the French Quarter and burned colonial government records held at the Cabildo. These fires predate your research window, but their effects run directly into the early 1800s by eliminating the colonial baseline that would have anchored genealogical research.

**Yellow fever epidemics** (especially severe in 1832, 1833, 1837, 1839, 1841, 1847) created registration *gaps*, not destruction: deaths occurred faster than clerks could record them, so epidemic-year death registrations are simply absent or thin. This is a record-creation failure, not a record-loss.

**Chronic moisture and flooding** caused ongoing paper deterioration in courthouse and sacristy holdings. The Louisiana State Archives led rescue microfilming efforts; some of those microfilmed copies are now on FamilySearch.

**The 1800 federal census is lost for Orleans Parish entirely.** Federal census research must start with 1810.

---

### What survived — and why

The key survivor is the **notarial archive**. Louisiana's civil law required a notary to create an official act for virtually every significant legal transaction: property sales, mortgages, contracts, wills, manumissions (freeing enslaved individuals), business partnerships, apprenticeships. Notaries held their own copies independently of the Cabildo — so when both fires hit, the notarial records were safe. The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds over 30 million pages dating to 1734. This is the primary substitute for almost everything that burned.

**St. Louis Cathedral's sacramental registers** also partially survived because some were held separately. Registers go back to 1731 (with gaps), and FamilySearch has digitized and indexed a large portion of them — see **FamilySearch collection 1612905** (Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925, ~988,000 records). Critically, the Cathedral kept **separate registers for enslaved individuals and free people of color** — these are essential for African-descended New Orleans families.

---

### Disaster-by-disaster substitute guide

| Disaster | What was lost | Where to look instead |
|---|---|---|
| Fires of 1788 & 1794 | Cabildo colonial records; some sacramental registers | Surviving St. Louis Cathedral registers; Notarial Archives; Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain) for pre-1803 families |
| Yellow fever gaps | Death registrations in epidemic years | Cemetery sexton records; newspaper death notices; succession (probate) inventories |
| Moisture/flood damage | Partial deterioration of paper records | FamilySearch microfilmed copies; Louisiana State Archives rescue microfilm |
| Lost 1800 federal census | Orleans Parish not recoverable | Tax lists; territorial records; notarial acts for presence evidence; start federal census work with 1810 |

---

### Key substitute sources

- **Notarial acts** — deeds, manumissions, contracts, wills. Physical at the Notarial Archives Research Center (in-person; partial online index). FamilySearch has one browse-only volume covering 1803–1820 (image group 004990115), not name-indexed.
- **Succession records** (Louisiana's term for probate) — inventories regularly name enslaved individuals with age, sometimes origin. FamilySearch collection 2078341 (Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984) has indexed images.
- **Newspapers** — obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, runaway slave advertisements (which describe enslaved individuals in physical detail and sometimes note family connections). Available on Newspapers.com and Chronicling America.
- **Military records** — the Battle of New Orleans (1814–15) generated service records for free men of color who served in organized battalions. NARA and Louisiana State Archives.
- **Archivo General de Indias, Seville** — for families present before 1803, colonial records that no longer exist locally may survive in Spain.

---

### Critical research warnings

1. **Louisiana uses civil-law terminology** — "succession" not "probate," "tutorship" not "guardianship." Wrong terms in online searches will miss results.
2. **Registers before ~1815 are in French or Spanish.** Searching in English misses them.
3. **Separate church registers exist** for enslaved individuals and free people of color at St. Louis Cathedral — don't assume a general register search is sufficient.
4. **The notarial archives are the starting point**, not a last resort. New Orleans notaries documented life the way courthouse records do in other states.

The locality entry has been saved to your project as `loc_001`.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana (1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Founded 1718 under French colonial authority; Spanish 1763–1800; Louisiana Purchase 1803; state of Louisiana 1812
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (city and parish coextensive)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Louisiana Territory (1803–1812), then State of Louisiana
- **Economy:** Major port — cotton, sugar, enslaved-person trade, shipping, banking
- **Ethnic composition:** Creole, Anglo-American, free people of color, enslaved African Americans, French/German/Irish/Caribbean immigrants
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant), Protestant denominations growing post-1803
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase (1803), Battle of New Orleans (1815), yellow fever epidemics, fires of 1788 and 1794

## Boundary changes
- Records 1803–1812 are territorial-era, held separately at the Louisiana State Archives
- Orleans Parish boundaries stable throughout 1800–1850
- Civil law (Napoleonic Code) throughout — produces unique record types vs. other US states

## Known record losses
| Disaster | Date | What was lost | Substitute sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| Great Fire | 1788 | Colonial records, some sacramental registers | Surviving St. Louis Cathedral registers; Archivo General de Indias, Seville |
| Second Great Fire | 1794 | Additional colonial records | Same; notarial archives survived |
| Yellow fever epidemics | 1832–1847 | Death registrations underrecorded | Cemetery records; newspapers; successions |
| Moisture/flood damage | Chronic | Partial paper record deterioration | FamilySearch microfilm; Louisiana State Archives rescue copies |

## Available record types

### Vital records
- No statewide civil birth registration existed for this period
- Sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral are the primary source (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps)
- FamilySearch: Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (collection 1612905) — indexed + images
- FamilySearch: Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (collection 1543892) — index only, no images
- Epidemic years underregistered

### Church records
- Denominations: Roman Catholic (primary); Protestant from post-1803
- Separate sacramental registers for enslaved individuals and free people of color at St. Louis Cathedral
- Language: French and Spanish through early 1800s; gradual shift to English
- Where held: Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives (originals); FamilySearch collection 1612905
- Digitization level: Indexed + images (collection 1612905, ~988,000 records)

### Notarial records
- Most important surviving record class; covers deeds, manumissions, contracts, wills, successions, mortgages
- New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center: 30+ million pages from 1734
- FamilySearch: 1 volume (imageGroupNumber 004990115), 167 images, 1803–1820, French/English — 0% indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image
- Remainder: physical only at the Notarial Archives

### Census records
- Federal: 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840 (head of household only); 1850 (names all free persons)
- 1800 federal census does not survive for Orleans Parish
- Digitization level: Indexed + images at Ancestry.com and FamilySearch

### Probate/succession records
- Louisiana term is 'succession'; tutorship = guardianship
- Inventories name enslaved individuals by name, age, sometimes origin
- FamilySearch: Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (collection 2078341) — indexed + images
- Originals: Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives

### Land records
- French arpent long-lot survey system
- Deeds executed before a notary; held at the Notarial Archives, not courthouse
- BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov): federal land patents, free and searchable
- Colonial Spanish grants: Archivo General de Indias, Seville

### Military records
- Battle of New Orleans (1814–1815); free men of color served in organized battalions
- NARA: federal service and pension records; Fold3.com (subscription)
- Louisiana State Archives: state militia records

### Cemetery records
- St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (est. 1789), No. 2 (est. 1823), Girod Street (Protestant, est. 1822)
- Find A Grave: partial coverage; sexton records more complete (Archdiocese archives)
- Epidemic years: mass burials with minimal documentation

### Newspaper records
- Le Moniteur de la Louisiane (French, 1794–1814); Louisiana Gazette (English, from 1804); Picayune (from 1837)
- Newspapers.com (subscription); Chronicling America (free)
- Runaway slave advertisements are a detailed source for enslaved individuals

### Immigration records
- Port of New Orleans passenger lists begin 1820 at NARA; Ancestry.com digitized
- Pre-1820: no systematic series; use notarial acts and naturalization records
- Naturalization: filed in Orleans Parish courts; Louisiana State Archives and NARA Southeast Region

### Enslaved persons records
- Succession inventories, notarial acts of sale, manumission acts, separate baptismal registers at St. Louis Cathedral, newspaper advertisements
- Key repositories: Notarial Archives (manumissions, sales); Archdiocese Archives (baptisms); Louisiana State Archives (successions)

## Repository guide

### Online
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1718–1925; Probate Records 1756–1984; Death Index 1819–1964; 1 notarial volume 1803–1820 | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Federal census; New Orleans passenger lists 1820+ | Subscription |
| Fold3.com | Military service and pension records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical New Orleans newspapers | Subscription |
| Chronicling America | Some early Louisiana papers | Free |
| BLM GLO | Federal land patents | Free |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30M+ pages notarial acts from 1734 | In-person |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Sacramental registers; burial records | By appointment |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial/state records, court records | In-person |
| NARA Southeast Region, Atlanta | Federal court, naturalization, military | In-person/request |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division | Newspapers, city directories, local history | In-person |
| Louisiana State Museum Library | Colonial/territorial records | In-person |

## Research tips
- Start with the Notarial Archives — nearly every legal life event was recorded there
- Use Louisiana-specific terminology in searches
- Church registers before 1815 are French/Spanish — search in the original language
- The 1800 federal census is lost for Orleans Parish; start with 1810
- Check the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) for pre-1803 family records
- Separate sacramental registers exist for enslaved individuals and free people of color
- Succession inventories name enslaved individuals — primary source for African American genealogy
- City directories from the 1820s supplement census records

Here is the complete guide, based on what the tools actually returned.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana (1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** New Orleans was founded 1718 under French colonial authority. Spain governed 1763–1800; France briefly retook it before the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 transferred it to the United States. Louisiana became a state in 1812. Orleans Parish has been the civil jurisdiction throughout the American period.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (city and parish are coextensive)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Louisiana Territory (1803–1812), then the State of Louisiana
- **Population during period:** The place_population tool returned no data for this location and period. The city was the largest in the American South during this era and grew rapidly through immigration and trade.
- **Economy:** Major port city — cotton, sugar, enslaved-person trade, shipping, commerce, banking
- **Ethnic composition:** Creole (French/Spanish descent), Anglo-American newcomers, free people of color (a legally distinct and substantial community), enslaved African Americans, and recent immigrants from France, Germany, Ireland, and the Caribbean
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant, administered through the Diocese of New Orleans and St. Louis Cathedral); Protestant denominations growing rapidly after 1803
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase (1803), Battle of New Orleans (1815), repeated yellow fever epidemics, devastating fires of 1788 and 1794

## Boundary changes

- Before 1803, records were created under French and Spanish colonial law administered through the Cabildo. These carry different organizational conventions from post-1803 American records and require separate search strategies.
- Territorial-era records (1803–1812) are held separately from state records at the Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge.
- Orleans Parish boundaries were stable throughout the 1800–1850 period.
- **Civil law note:** Louisiana uses civil law (Napoleonic Code) rather than the common law of other US states. This produces unique record types — successions instead of probate estates, tutorships instead of guardianships — and researchers must use Louisiana-specific terminology when searching online databases.

## Known record losses: Disasters

Understanding what was destroyed and what survived is the prerequisite to every search strategy here.

**Fires of 1788 and 1794**
Both fires occurred before 1800, but their effects run directly into the early 1800s:
- The 1788 fire destroyed approximately 856 buildings and an unknown quantity of colonial governmental records held in the Cabildo.
- The 1794 fire destroyed much of the rebuilt quarter and additional records.
- Many colonial-era administrative records that would have anchored early 1800s genealogical research — property history, earlier sacramental register copies — do not survive.
- The sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral were partially preserved because some were held separately from the Cabildo. Registers dating to 1731 exist, though with gaps.
- The notarial archives survived both fires because notarial offices held their own copies independently of the Cabildo. This is the most critical survival fact for this jurisdiction.

**Yellow fever epidemics**
Repeated epidemics — particularly severe in 1832, 1833, 1837, 1839, 1841, and 1847 — killed large portions of the population rapidly. Deaths occurred faster than clerks could register them; epidemic-year death registrations are incomplete or absent. This is a record-creation gap, not a destruction: the events were not recorded at the time.

**Floods and moisture damage**
New Orleans sits below sea level. Paper records held in parish courthouses and church sacristies suffered chronic water damage over decades. The Louisiana State Archives has been the primary rescue institution; some damaged records were microfilmed before further deterioration.

**What survived:** Per the wiki_search result for this query (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters), the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734. Notarial records are the exceptional survivor class and the primary substitute source for nearly everything that burned.

## Available record types

For each type, note that the all four wiki_place_page sections for Louisiana returned only a generic redirect page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Research_Guide) rather than Louisiana-specific content. The same happened for all seven constructed-URL wiki_read calls. All specific dates, level designations, and institutional details below come from the wiki_search chunks and tool results actually returned — not from those redirected pages. Researchers should consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Vital_Records and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy directly for dates the tools did not return.

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Civil registration start:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Louisiana Vital Records page was not retrievable in this session (redirected to a generic page). The FamilySearch Wiki should be consulted directly for the confirmed level and date.
- **What exists for 1800–1850:** No statewide civil birth registration existed for this period. Sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral are the main source for baptisms, marriages, and burials.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (collection 1612905) — indexed + images, ~988,000 records, ~494,000 images. https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905
- **Death index:** Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (collection 1543892) — index only, no images. https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892. Note that epidemic death years have significant gaps.
- **Marriage collection:** Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 (collection 1798054) — indexed + images, covers the later portion of the target period. https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054
- **Gaps:** Epidemic years are underregistered. The 1788 and 1794 fires created gaps in earlier registers that carry into incomplete sequences for the early 1800s.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Notarial records, succession records, cemetery records, newspaper notices

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (primary, through St. Louis Cathedral and later satellite parishes); Protestant churches established in growing numbers after the Louisiana Purchase
- **Record types:** Baptisms (include legitimacy status and, for enslaved individuals, the owner's name), marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Enslaved and free people of color:** St. Louis Cathedral maintained separate registers for enslaved individuals and free people of color. These are among the most important sources for researching African-descended New Orleans families in this period. The owner's name recorded for enslaved persons is a critical linking fact.
- **Language:** Records are primarily in French and Spanish through the early 1800s, shifting gradually to English after 1803. Researchers must be able to read French, or use translation assistance.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives (originals); FamilySearch collection 1612905 (microfilmed and digitized)
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 1612905)

### Notarial records

This is the single most important surviving record class for early New Orleans and has no parallel in other US states.

- **What they are:** Under Louisiana civil law, a notary was required to create an official act for nearly every significant legal transaction: property sales, mortgages, contracts, manumissions (freeing of enslaved individuals), apprenticeships, business partnerships, wills, successions, and more. These acts are the documentary backbone of New Orleans society.
- **Volume:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734, per the wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters.
- **FamilySearch volume:** 1 digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 004990115), 167 images, covering 1803–1820, in French and English. This volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be browsed image by image with no search capability.
- **Digitization level:** Browse-only images for the one FamilySearch volume; the vast majority of notarial holdings are physical only at the Notarial Archives Research Center.
- **Manumission records:** Because manumissions required a notarial act, the notarial archives are the primary source for documenting the freedom of enslaved individuals.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840 cover New Orleans, listing heads of household with members counted by age/sex/race categories (not named below the head). The 1850 census is the first to name every free person.
- **Critical gap:** The 1800 federal census does not survive for Orleans Parish. Federal census research must begin with 1810.
- **State/territorial census:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Louisiana Census page was not retrievable in this session. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Census for the full list of state enumerations.
- **Digitization level:** Federal censuses indexed and available at Ancestry.com (subscription) and FamilySearch (free)

### Probate and succession records

- **Louisiana terminology:** The equivalent of probate is a "succession" (testate if a will exists, intestate if not). Guardianship equivalents are "tutorships." These are filed in civil district court, not a probate court.
- **What they contain:** Inventories of estates, which in this period regularly list enslaved individuals by name, age, and sometimes origin — making succession records a critical source for African American genealogy.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (collection 2078341) — indexed + images, ~457,000 records, ~228,000 images. https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341
- **Where originals are held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 2078341)

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses the French arpent system (long-lot surveys running perpendicular to waterways) — not the rectangular township-range system of other states. Property descriptions in deeds look very different.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under Spanish and French colonial rule, land grants were issued by colonial governors. After 1803, the US General Land Office confirmed existing grants and issued new ones. The BLM General Land Office Records website (glorecords.blm.gov) holds federal land patents.
- **Types:** Notarial acts (deeds, mortgages), Spanish/French land grants, US land patents, tax records
- **Key point:** Because deeds were executed before a notary rather than recorded at a courthouse, the New Orleans Notarial Archives holds the primary deed record — not the parish clerk of court. Searching only courthouse deed books will miss most property transactions.
- **Colonial grants:** Records of the Spanish colonial government sent to Spain survive at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville — a significant source for pre-1803 land history.
- **Digitization level:** The one FamilySearch notarial volume is browse-only; BLM GLO patents are free and searchable online; the majority of notarial land acts are physical only.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Battle of New Orleans (1814–1815); various territorial militia actions
- **Notable:** Free men of color served in organized battalions in the Battle of New Orleans — records of these units exist and are a significant source for that community.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files at NARA; state militia records at Louisiana State Archives
- **Where held:** NARA (federal service and pension records); Louisiana State Archives (state militia); Fold3.com (many NARA records digitized)
- **Digitization level:** Federal pension and service records partially indexed at Fold3.com and Ancestry.com

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (est. 1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (est. 1823), Girod Street Cemetery (Protestant, est. 1822). Above-ground tomb burials are the local practice, a distinctive feature that affects how burial records read.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has substantial but not complete coverage
- **Physical records:** Sexton and burial records held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives
- **Epidemic burials:** During yellow fever epidemics, mass burials occurred with minimal individual documentation — some of the worst gaps in the record.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Le Moniteur de la Louisiane (French, 1794–1814); Louisiana Gazette (English, from 1804); New Orleans Picayune (from 1837), and others
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage announcements, legal notices (estate sales, sheriff's sales, manumission notices), shipping arrivals, and runaway slave advertisements — which describe enslaved individuals in physical detail and sometimes note family connections
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Museum Library; Louisiana Division of the New Orleans Public Library; Newspapers.com (subscription, https://www.newspapers.com/); Chronicling America (free, chroniclingamerica.loc.gov)

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Port of New Orleans:** One of the busiest ports in North America. Systematic passenger arrival lists begin in 1820 at NARA.
- **Pre-1820 arrivals:** No systematic passenger list series exists for New Orleans before 1820. Notarial acts and naturalization records are the substitutes.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record. In New Orleans this means Orleans Parish courts. The Louisiana State Archives and NARA's Southeast Region facility (Atlanta) hold these records.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest — children as young as newborns are listed.
- **Digitization level:** Ancestry.com has New Orleans passenger lists from 1820; NARA (archives.gov) has some coverage. Pre-1820: no series exists.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Property tax and personal property tax at the parish level
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can establish presence between census years and document property holdings; they partially substitute for the lost 1800 census
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives; Orleans Parish Assessor's Office
- **Digitization level:** Largely physical only for this period; some microfilmed holdings at FamilySearch

### Enslaved persons records

- **Sources:** Succession inventories (name, age, sometimes origin), notarial acts of sale (transfers of enslaved persons), manumission acts, baptismal registers at St. Louis Cathedral (separate registers), runaway slave advertisements in newspapers, and city tax records that sometimes list enslaved individuals
- **Key repositories:** New Orleans Notarial Archives (sale acts, manumissions); Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives (baptismal registers); Louisiana State Archives (successions)
- **Note:** The federal slave schedules of 1850 do not name enslaved individuals — only age, sex, and description are given there. The notarial and church sources are far more informative.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (1612905); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 (1798054); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (2078341); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (1543892); 1 notarial volume 1803–1820 (browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | US Federal Census (1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850); New Orleans passenger lists (1820+) | Subscription |
| Fold3.com | Federal military service and pension records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical New Orleans newspapers | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (loc.gov) | Some early Louisiana newspapers | Free |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Finding aids; some digitized records | Free/varies |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for Orleans Parish covering 1803–1820 (totalResults: 1), which is the complete FamilySearch digitized volume set for this place and period as indexed. This almost certainly reflects a digitization gap rather than an absence of records — the New Orleans Notarial Archives alone holds tens of millions of pages not yet digitized.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734, including deeds, mortgages, manumissions, successions | In-person; partial index online |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Original sacramental registers; burial records | In-person by appointment |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and state records, court records, microfilm | In-person; online catalog |
| NARA Southeast Region, Atlanta | Federal court records, naturalization, some military | In-person; records request |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Succession/civil court records | In-person; some transferred to State Archives |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division | Newspapers, city directories, local history | In-person; some digitized |
| Louisiana State Museum Library | Colonial and territorial records, newspapers | In-person |

## Records NOT online

- The overwhelming majority of notarial acts (deeds, manumissions, contracts, most wills) — physical only at the Notarial Archives Research Center
- Most original sacramental registers (beyond what FamilySearch has microfilmed)
- Parish-level tax records for this period
- Orleans Parish civil court records from this period beyond what is in FamilySearch collection 2078341
- Pre-1820 passenger records (they do not exist as a systematic series)
- Territorial-era administrative records at the Louisiana State Archives

## Known record losses

| Disaster | Date | What was lost | Substitute sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| Great Fire of New Orleans | 1788 | ~856 structures; Cabildo-held colonial records; some sacramental registers | Surviving St. Louis Cathedral registers; Archivo General de Indias, Seville |
| Second Great Fire | 1794 | Additional French Quarter structures and records | Same; notarial archives survived because held separately |
| Yellow fever epidemics | 1832, 1833, 1837, 1839, 1841, 1847 | Death registrations underrecorded during outbreaks | Cemetery sexton records; newspaper death notices; succession records |
| Moisture/flood damage | Chronic throughout period | Partial deterioration of paper records | Microfilmed copies at FamilySearch; Louisiana State Archives rescue microfilm programs |
| 1800 federal census | Lost | Orleans Parish not recoverable | Begin federal census research with 1810; use territorial records and tax lists for 1800s context |

## Research tips

- **The notarial archives are the starting point.** In New Orleans, a notary documented every legally significant life event. Begin there before concluding a record does not exist. (Source: wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)
- **Use Louisiana-specific terminology.** "Succession" not "probate," "tutorship" not "guardianship," "interdiction" not "incompetency." Wrong terms in online searches consistently miss results.
- **Church register language.** Registers before roughly 1815 are predominantly in French or Spanish. Searching in English misses these entries. Learn the standard French phrases (baptême, mariage, sépulture) or work with someone who can read them.
- **Separate registers exist for enslaved individuals and free people of color** at St. Louis Cathedral. Do not assume a single search of the general register is sufficient for African-descended families.
- **Enslaved persons are named in notarial acts and succession inventories.** These are more reliable and detailed than census slave schedules, which name no enslaved individual below the slaveholder.
- **Runaway slave advertisements** in newspapers contain physical descriptions and sometimes note family connections, language, and origin — a significant source for enslaved individuals.
- **The 1800 census is lost for Orleans Parish.** Begin federal census research with 1810. Use tax lists and notarial records for presence evidence before 1810.
- **Search the Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain)** for families present before 1803. Colonial records that no longer exist locally survive in Spain.
- **City directories** from the 1820s onward place individuals at specific addresses between census years.
- **Free men of color military service:** Units of free Black men served at the Battle of New Orleans — their service records are at NARA and the Louisiana State Archives, and are a significant research source for that community.
- **For families near the parish line:** Adjacent parishes (St. Bernard, Jefferson, St. Charles) may hold records for families living near the Orleans Parish boundary; search all of them.
- **Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly** for Louisiana at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy — the Louisiana-specific wiki pages were not retrievable in this session and contain research guidance not captured here.

New Orleans in the early 1800s is a jurisdiction where the disaster history is inseparable from the research strategy. Two major fires in the 1790s destroyed much of the colonial governmental record base, and repeated yellow fever epidemics in the 1830s and 1840s created registration gaps precisely when the city's population was growing fastest. The good news is that the notarial system — legally required acts prepared by notaries for virtually every property sale, contract, manumission, and will — survived both fires because notaries kept their own copies. That archive (30+ million pages) is now the primary substitute for most of what burned, and it is held at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center. For church records, St. Louis Cathedral's sacramental registers go back to 1731 with gaps, and FamilySearch has digitized and indexed a large portion of them. The most important warnings are: the 1800 federal census is lost for this parish, so start with 1810; civil registration in the modern sense did not exist yet; and all record searches require using Louisiana's civil-law terminology rather than common-law terms. The next step would be building a research plan that sequences these sources for the specific ancestor you are trying to trace.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana (1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Founded 1718 under French colonial authority; Spanish 1763–1800; Louisiana Purchase 1803; state of Louisiana 1812
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (city and parish coextensive)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Louisiana Territory (1803–1812), then State of Louisiana
- **Economy:** Major port — cotton, sugar, enslaved-person trade, shipping, banking
- **Ethnic composition:** Creole, Anglo-American, free people of color, enslaved African Americans, French/German/Irish/Caribbean immigrants
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant), Protestant denominations growing post-1803
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase (1803), Battle of New Orleans (1815), yellow fever epidemics, fires of 1788 and 1794

## Boundary changes
- Records 1803–1812 are territorial-era, held separately at the Louisiana State Archives
- Orleans Parish boundaries stable throughout 1800–1850
- Civil law (Napoleonic Code) throughout — produces unique record types vs. other US states

## Known record losses
| Disaster | Date | What was lost | Substitute sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| Great Fire | 1788 | Colonial records, some sacramental registers | Surviving St. Louis Cathedral registers; Archivo General de Indias, Seville |
| Second Great Fire | 1794 | Additional colonial records | Same; notarial archives survived |
| Yellow fever epidemics | 1832–1847 | Death registrations underrecorded | Cemetery records; newspapers; successions |
| Moisture/flood damage | Chronic | Partial paper record deterioration | FamilySearch microfilm; Louisiana State Archives rescue copies |

## Available record types

### Vital records
- No statewide civil birth registration existed for this period
- Sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral are the primary source (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps)
- FamilySearch: Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (collection 1612905) — indexed + images
- FamilySearch: Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 (collection 1543892) — index only, no images
- Epidemic years underregistered

### Church records
- Denominations: Roman Catholic (primary); Protestant from post-1803
- Separate sacramental registers for enslaved individuals and free people of color at St. Louis Cathedral
- Language: French and Spanish through early 1800s; gradual shift to English
- Where held: Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives (originals); FamilySearch collection 1612905
- Digitization level: Indexed + images (collection 1612905, ~988,000 records)

### Notarial records
- Most important surviving record class; covers deeds, manumissions, contracts, wills, successions, mortgages
- New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center: 30+ million pages from 1734
- FamilySearch: 1 volume (imageGroupNumber 004990115), 167 images, 1803–1820, French/English — 0% indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image
- Remainder: physical only at the Notarial Archives

### Census records
- Federal: 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840 (head of household only); 1850 (names all free persons)
- 1800 federal census does not survive for Orleans Parish
- Digitization level: Indexed + images at Ancestry.com and FamilySearch

### Probate/succession records
- Louisiana term is 'succession'; tutorship = guardianship
- Inventories name enslaved individuals by name, age, sometimes origin
- FamilySearch: Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (collection 2078341) — indexed + images
- Originals: Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives

### Land records
- French arpent long-lot survey system
- Deeds executed before a notary; held at the Notarial Archives, not courthouse
- BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov): federal land patents, free and searchable
- Colonial Spanish grants: Archivo General de Indias, Seville

### Military records
- Battle of New Orleans (1814–1815); free men of color served in organized battalions
- NARA: federal service and pension records; Fold3.com (subscription)
- Louisiana State Archives: state militia records

### Cemetery records
- St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (est. 1789), No. 2 (est. 1823), Girod Street (Protestant, est. 1822)
- Find A Grave: partial coverage; sexton records more complete (Archdiocese archives)
- Epidemic years: mass burials with minimal documentation

### Newspaper records
- Le Moniteur de la Louisiane (French, 1794–1814); Louisiana Gazette (English, from 1804); Picayune (from 1837)
- Newspapers.com (subscription); Chronicling America (free)
- Runaway slave advertisements are a detailed source for enslaved individuals

### Immigration records
- Port of New Orleans passenger lists begin 1820 at NARA; Ancestry.com digitized
- Pre-1820: no systematic series; use notarial acts and naturalization records
- Naturalization: filed in Orleans Parish courts; Louisiana State Archives and NARA Southeast Region

### Enslaved persons records
- Succession inventories, notarial acts of sale, manumission acts, separate baptismal registers at St. Louis Cathedral, newspaper advertisements
- Key repositories: Notarial Archives (manumissions, sales); Archdiocese Archives (baptisms); Louisiana State Archives (successions)

## Repository guide

### Online
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1718–1925; Probate Records 1756–1984; Death Index 1819–1964; 1 notarial volume 1803–1820 | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Federal census; New Orleans passenger lists 1820+ | Subscription |
| Fold3.com | Military service and pension records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical New Orleans newspapers | Subscription |
| Chronicling America | Some early Louisiana papers | Free |
| BLM GLO | Federal land patents | Free |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30M+ pages notarial acts from 1734 | In-person |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Sacramental registers; burial records | By appointment |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial/state records, court records | In-person |
| NARA Southeast Region, Atlanta | Federal court, naturalization, military | In-person/request |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division | Newspapers, city directories, local history | In-person |
| Louisiana State Museum Library | Colonial/territorial records | In-person |

## Research tips
- Start with the Notarial Archives — nearly every legal life event was recorded there
- Use Louisiana-specific terminology in searches
- Church registers before 1815 are French/Spanish — search in the original language
- The 1800 federal census is lost for Orleans Parish; start with 1810
- Check the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) for pre-1803 family records
- Separate sacramental registers exist for enslaved individuals and free people of color
- Succession inventories name enslaved individuals — primary source for African American genealogy
- City directories from the 1820s supplement census records

---

- **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** — Catholic parish registers frequently record the Irish parish or townland for adults who arrived as Famine refugees. Contact them directly for access.
- **National Archives, Waltham, MA** — Holds undigitized immigration and naturalization records for New England.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts — Immigration Records (1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Place surveyed:** Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States
- **Type:** City and port of entry; part of Suffolk County
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Massachusetts
- **Population during period:** By 1850 over a quarter of residents were Irish-born (Great Famine, 1845-1852). Boston was the primary New England port of entry.
- **Economy:** Maritime trade, manufacturing, commerce.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish influx; also English, German, Canadian arrivals; earlier Yankee Protestant majority.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist, Episcopalian, Catholic, Methodist, Baptist.
- **Key historical events:** Irish Famine immigration surge 1845-1852.

## Boundary changes
Suffolk County established 1643; no boundary change affected Boston's jurisdictional identity in the 1840s.

## Available record types

### Passenger lists
- Date range: 1820-1891 (FamilySearch collection 1784312)
- 1840s lists record name, age, sex, occupation, country of origin only
- One digitized volume confirmed: image group 003345210 (389 images, 1840-1850); 3% name-indexed, full-text searchable — mostly browse-only
- Originals at NARA Boston (Waltham), RG 36
- Access: FamilySearch (free); Ancestry (subscription)

### Naturalization records
- FamilySearch collection 1459213 (1790-1906); indexed + images
- Declarations of Intention often name country/town of birth, arrival date, ship
- Filed in any court of record: Suffolk County courts and federal courts
- Originals at NARA Boston and Massachusetts State Archives

### Vital records
- Town-level registration; FamilySearch collection 2061550 (1620-1890); indexed + images
- Originals at Massachusetts State Archives and City of Boston Registry Division

### Church records
- FamilySearch collection 1921657 (1630-1920); indexed + images
- Catholic parish registers at Archdiocese of Boston Archives (some undigitized)
- Often name Irish parish/townland of origin

### Census records
- 1840 federal census (head of household only)
- 1850 federal census (names every individual; records country of birth) — critical for immigrant families
- Both indexed on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry

### Probate records
- FamilySearch collection 1678901 (1635-1991); indexed + images
- Can name surviving family in Ireland

### The Pilot Missing Persons Database
- Free indexed database at infowanted.bc.edu
- Covers 1831-1921; specifically for Irish immigrants through Boston
- Often names Irish county or parish of origin

### Newspaper records
- The Pilot (Boston): Missing Persons column; digitized run at Boston College Burns Library
- Other Boston papers: Boston Daily Atlas, Boston Daily Advertiser
- Access: infowanted.bc.edu (free); Newspapers.com, GenealogyBank (subscription); Boston Public Library microfilm

### Cemetery records
- Major Catholic cemeteries: Holy Cross (Malden), St. Augustine's (South Boston)
- Online: FindAGrave (free)
- Sexton records at individual cemetery offices; Catholic burial registers at Archdiocese of Boston Archives

## Repository guide

### Online
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Passenger Lists 1784312; Naturalization 1459213; Vital Records 2061550; Church Records 1921657; Probate 1678901 | Free |
| Ancestry | Passenger lists; naturalization; federal censuses; vital records | Subscription |
| infowanted.bc.edu | The Pilot Missing Persons Database 1831-1921 | Free |
| Newspapers.com / GenealogyBank | Historical Boston newspapers | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records; some passenger list images | Subscription |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| NARA Boston (Waltham, MA) | Customs passenger lists RG 36; federal court naturalization RG 21 | In-person |
| Massachusetts State Archives | State/county court naturalizations; state vital records | In-person |
| Boston City Archives | Municipal records; tax assessments | In-person |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers 1840s onward | Written inquiry |
| Boston Public Library | Newspaper microfilm; city directories | In-person |
| NEHGS (AmericanAncestors.org) | Compiled vital records; manuscript collections | Membership/subscription |

## Records NOT online
- Most undigitized Catholic parish registers (contact Archdiocese of Boston Archives)
- Boston City Archives tax assessments for most years
- Suffolk County court minute books (naturalization proceedings not yet indexed)
- Individual cemetery sexton records

## Known record losses
No major catastrophic loss documented for Suffolk County records in this period. Customs passenger lists have gaps and some deterioration. Pre-1906 naturalization records are scattered across multiple courts with no exhaustive single index.

## Research tips
- Start with the 1850 federal census: names every household member, records country of birth
- The Pilot Missing Persons Database (infowanted.bc.edu) is high priority for Irish immigrants
- 1840s passenger lists give country of origin only — not hometown; work backward through naturalization declarations and church records
- Check the full manifest page around any passenger list hit for family members
- Catholic baptismal and marriage registers often name the Irish parish or townland of origin
- Pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court — search Suffolk County courts and federal courts
- NEHGS/AmericanAncestors.org holds Massachusetts-specific compiled records not available elsewhere online
