# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1860-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Allegheny County formed 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland Counties. Pittsburgh incorporated as a city 1816.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the population tool for this place in this period — the tool returned an empty result. Pittsburgh's industrial growth was documented in the federal censuses of 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900 (1890 is almost entirely destroyed).
- **Economy:** Iron and steel production, glass manufacturing, coal mining, coke production, railroad operations. The Carnegie Steel Company and Jones & Laughlin Steel were dominant employers by the 1880s-1890s. The confluence of three rivers and access to Connellsville coke made Allegheny County the center of American steel output.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large waves of Irish, German (established by mid-century), then Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Hungarian, Italian, and other Southern and Eastern European immigrants arriving from the 1880s onward, recruited directly for mill labor.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (multiple national parishes — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, Lithuanian), Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran, Episcopal, Jewish congregations. National parishes organized by ethnic community are the key genealogical unit.
- **Key historical events:** Great Pittsburgh Fire (1845, destroyed much of downtown — some early records lost); Homestead Strike (1892, Carnegie Steel); Johnstown Flood (1889 — upstream, but relevant to regional research).

## Boundary changes

Allegheny County boundaries have been stable since 1800. The City of Pittsburgh annexed the neighboring City of Allegheny (across the Allegheny River) in 1907 — just outside the target period, but records created by or for residents of Allegheny City before 1907 are held under that separate municipality. If your research extends slightly past 1900, note that what was "Allegheny City" became Pittsburgh's North Side after annexation.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start dates:**
  - **County-level birth and death registration:** Allegheny County began registering births and deaths at the county level around **1870**, according to the FamilySearch Wiki ([Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)). Philadelphia began in 1860; other counties are variable.
  - **Statewide registration:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until **1906** ([Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)). The statewide 1906 series is well-preserved; the county-level pre-1906 records are spottier.
  - **Marriage records:** Kept at the county level from the colonial era. Marriage licenses and bonds are at the Allegheny County courthouse. FamilySearch holds the collection "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950" (collection ID 1921317, 524,189 records, images available) and "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950" (collection ID 1571957, 312,045 records).
  - **Death certificates:** "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968" (collection ID 2255317, 4,218,763 indexed records with images) begins after the target period but covers any family member who died after 1906. These are highly detailed and include father's name, mother's maiden name, and birthplace — extremely useful for tracing immigrant origins.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse (originals for pre-1906 county registrations); Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) for statewide series; FamilySearch online for the digitized collections above.
- **Gaps:** For births and deaths in the 1860s-1870s, the Allegheny County registration was just beginning and compliance was inconsistent. For the period before 1870, church records are the primary substitute.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers — see Church Records below. Family Bibles. Newspaper notices.

### Church records

This is one of the most critical record classes for the Pittsburgh steel-era population. The massive immigrant workforce organized itself by ethnicity into **national parishes**, meaning a Slovak Catholic parish, a Polish Catholic parish, and an Irish Catholic parish might all exist in the same mill neighborhood — each keeping its own registers, in its own language.

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant among later immigrants), Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran (German), Episcopal, Greek Catholic (Ruthenian/Ukrainian), Serbian Orthodox, Jewish congregations.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (often recording both parents' full names and sometimes village of origin in the old country), marriages, burials, confirmations. Confirmation records are dated separately from baptism and can establish an approximate birth year for children whose birth record doesn't survive.
- **Where held:** Many registers remain with individual parishes. Diocesan archives (Diocese of Pittsburgh, Roman Catholic) hold older or closed-parish records. FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania church records. The FamilySearch Wiki notes that Catholic parishes for specific ethnic communities (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian) are often the best source for family data for the immigrant generation. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records))
- **Language:** Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, and Latin registers are common. A researcher must be able to read the original language or find a translation aid.
- **Digitization level:** Varies widely. Some are microfilmed by FamilySearch (browse-only); others remain physical only at the parish or diocesan archive.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 are available and name every household member with age, birthplace, and occupation. The **1880 and 1900 censuses** are fully indexed and searchable on Ancestry and FamilySearch. The **1870 census** is indexed. The **1860 census** is indexed. The **1890 census is almost entirely destroyed** — a fire at the Commerce Department in 1921 destroyed approximately 99% of the schedules nationwide.
- **1880 census industry schedules:** The 1880 Manufactures Schedule enumerated factories, their output, number of employees, and wages. This is not a name index of workers but gives context about the mills your ancestor may have worked in.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for 1860, 1870, and 1880 — record deaths in the 12 months preceding the census date. Useful for finding family members who died between registrations.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a statewide census between federal enumerations. There is no Pennsylvania state census to substitute for the missing 1890 federal records.
- **Occupation column:** The 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal censuses all include an occupation column. For the 1880 and 1900 censuses this is searchable. For immigrants arriving in the 1880s-1890s, the **1900 census** is especially useful — it added columns for year of immigration, years in the United States, and citizenship status.
- **Access:** Indexed + images on Ancestry (subscription) and FamilySearch (free). FamilySearch held 3 digitized volumes for this search (vol. 008120441: Probate, 1683-1994, 1,180 images, browse-only; vol. 008120442: Death Records 1852-1968, 674 images, browse-only; vol. 008120443: Naturalization Records 1790-1915, 351 images, 15% indexed, English/German).

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, inventories, guardianship files. For mill workers, probate records are often the best evidence of a family's structure and real estate holdings after a worker was killed or died of an industrial accident.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Register of Wills (county courthouse, Pittsburgh). FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collection ID 1999196) has 3,200,560 images but **0 indexed records** — this is a browse-only collection. You must browse image by image without a name search.
- **Court records:** The Court of Common Pleas holds naturalization petitions (pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record), name changes, civil suits, and guardianships. Naturalization records at the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia document the immigrant steel worker population. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records))
- **FamilySearch volume:** Vol. 008120443 covers Pennsylvania Naturalization Records 1790-1915, 351 images, 15% name-indexed, English and German. This is the only partially searchable volume returned.
- **Digitization level:** Probate images — browse-only (0% indexed). Naturalization records — partially indexed (15%).

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a state-land (not federal-land) state. The original grants derive from William Penn's Land Office, not the federal BLM General Land Office.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania Land Office in Harrisburg holds warrant, survey, and patent records dating from Penn's proprietorship (1681). The FamilySearch Wiki confirms this ([Pennsylvania Land and Probate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)).
- **County deeds:** Held at the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds. County deed books begin from the county's formation (1788).
- **Tax records (assessment lists, tax duplicates):** Pennsylvania tax records survive from the 1690s in some counties and serve as census substitutes. For Allegheny County, tax lists from the late 18th and 19th centuries are held at the county courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives. They are particularly useful as a substitute for the missing 1890 census.
- **Types relevant to this period:** Property deeds (mill workers buying row houses or city lots), tax assessment records, mortgages.
- **Digitization level:** Not indexed online in significant volume for this period; primarily physical or microfilm at the courthouse and state archives.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861-1865) is the dominant military event for this period. The Spanish-American War (1898) is at the end of the period.
- **Record types:**
  - Civil War service records and pension files at NARA. Pennsylvania pension files are especially rich — a widow's pension application often records marriage date, children's names and ages, and detailed family history.
  - Civil War draft registrations (1863 Enrollment Act) list all men 20-45, with age, occupation, and birthplace — a valuable substitute source for men who do not appear in the 1860 census by name.
  - Grand Army of the Republic (GAR) membership records for veterans.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, DC and the regional facility at Philadelphia for some Pennsylvania records). Fold3 (fold3.com) has Civil War pension index cards and many service records, subscription required. FamilySearch has some digitized Civil War records.
- **Immigrant steel workers and military:** Many immigrants who arrived in the 1880s-1890s were not subject to the Civil War draft but may appear in the Spanish-American War or later registrations. Their military records, if any, date from 1898 onward.

### Occupational and industrial records (the key focus for this survey)

This is the distinctive record class for Pittsburgh's steel era. These records are **not** typically found on FamilySearch or Ancestry and require direct contact with specialized repositories.

- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary survival. Some Carnegie Steel and related company records survive at the **Heinz History Center** (Senator John Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh — the Smithsonian affiliate for western Pennsylvania history) and the **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives**. These may include hiring books, payroll ledgers, and accident records. The FamilySearch Wiki confirms this directly: "company employment records (fragmentary — some survive at the Heinz History Center and the Rivers of Steel archives)." ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Industrial and Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records))
- **Union membership records:** The Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers (founded 1876) organized skilled workers in Pittsburgh mills before the Homestead Strike (1892). Post-1892 the union was largely broken at Carnegie plants; the United Steelworkers (USWA) succeeded it in the 1930s. Union records, where they survive, are held by the union archives or donated to university labor collections. The **University of Pittsburgh's Archives Service Center** and the **Pennsylvania State University's Special Collections** hold labor organization records.
- **State factory inspector reports:** The Pennsylvania Bureau of Industrial Statistics published annual reports from 1873 onward listing factories, their locations, number of employees, and sometimes nationality of the workforce. These are not individual name indexes but establish which mills were operating and the demographics of their workers. The Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds these.
- **City directories:** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds Pittsburgh city directories from the 1810s forward. City directories list head of household with occupation and street address, making them an annual substitute for the census. They are the most practical tool for tracking a steel worker year-by-year between census enumerations. They are **not** fully indexed online for this period — many must be consulted in person at the Carnegie Library or on microfilm. The FamilySearch Wiki confirms the Carnegie Library's directory holdings. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Industrial and Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records))
- **Accident and coroner's records:** Industrial accidents were common. The Allegheny County Coroner's records document deaths from industrial accidents and may include testimony from co-workers and supervisors naming the mill, the job, and the circumstances. These are held at the Allegheny County courthouse.
- **Digitization level:** Industrial and occupational records are almost entirely **physical only**. City directories exist on microfilm at the Carnegie Library. No significant portion is name-indexed online.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery (Pittsburgh, est. 1844), St. Mary's Cemetery, Calvary Cemetery (Catholic), and many ethnic/denominational cemeteries associated with national parishes.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has significant coverage of Pittsburgh-area cemeteries, free to search. BillionGraves also has entries. Coverage is uneven — major Protestant cemeteries are better represented than smaller Catholic or ethnic cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemeteries. Catholic burial records are often recorded in the parish register, not just the cemetery office.
- **Access:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves are free and online. Sexton records are physical-only at the cemetery office.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Pittsburgh Gazette (founded 1786, one of the oldest newspapers west of the Alleghenies), Pittsburgh Post, Pittsburgh Dispatch, Pittsburgh Press, and ethnic-language papers (Slovak, Polish, Croatian newspapers serving the immigrant communities by the 1890s).
- **Where held:** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds extensive newspaper microfilm. Newspapers.com (subscription) has historical Pittsburgh newspapers. The Library of Congress Chronicling America project (free at chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) has some Pennsylvania papers for this period.
- **Content value:** Obituaries often the only death notice for a worker. Marriage notices. Legal notices (estate settlements, sheriff's sales). Accident reports from mills name workers. Strike coverage names union leaders and workers. Ethnic-language papers may carry community news not in the English press.
- **Digitization level:** Partial. Major English papers partly indexed on Newspapers.com (subscription). Ethnic-language papers are largely undigitized and must be consulted on microfilm at the Carnegie Library or the Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** The vast majority of Eastern and Southern European immigrants entering Pittsburgh's mills arrived through **New York (Ellis Island, 1892-1957; Castle Garden, 1820-1892)**. Some came through Baltimore or Philadelphia.
- **Record types:**
  - Passenger arrival manifests: Post-1895 manifests at Ellis Island are name-indexed and searchable free at Ancestry and the Ellis Island Foundation (libertyellisfoundation.org). Pre-1895 Castle Garden manifests are searchable at castlegarden.org.
  - **Naturalization records:** Pre-1906, a man could naturalize in any court of record — Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas, federal courts, or even justice-of-the-peace courts. The FamilySearch vol. 008120443 covers Pennsylvania Naturalization Records 1790-1915 (351 images, 15% indexed). Post-1906 naturalizations moved to federal courts (NARA Philadelphia).
  - Declaration of Intention ("first papers") and Petition for Naturalization ("second papers"): These often record the immigrant's town of origin, which is essential for locating church records in the home country.
  - **Alien registration:** Not required until 1940 (Alien Registration Act), outside this period.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed. Post-1906 manifests added a contact person in the United States and in the country of origin, often naming the specific village.
- **Where held:** NARA; online at Ancestry (subscription) and Ancestry's free Ellis Island partition; FamilySearch.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Property tax assessment lists, personal property schedules.
- **Date range:** Pennsylvania tax records survive from the colonial period. For Allegheny County in the 1860s-1900s, annual tax assessment lists are held at the Allegheny County courthouse and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** With the 1890 federal census almost entirely destroyed, the **1890 city directory and county tax assessment lists** are the primary tools for locating a Pittsburgh resident in that decade. Tax lists name the property owner and assessed value — they will not capture renters who owned no property, which includes many newly arrived mill workers.

The following record types exist but are not available in any significant online name-indexed database for this place and period:

- **Company employment records** (Heinz History Center, Rivers of Steel) — physical only, fragmentary survival
- **City directories** for most years between census enumerations — microfilm at Carnegie Library; not name-indexed online
- **Allegheny County coroner's records** — physical at courthouse
- **Pennsylvania factory inspector reports** — physical at Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Ethnic-language newspapers** (Slovak, Polish, Croatian) — microfilm at Carnegie Library; not digitized

- **Catholic parish registers** (many) — physical at individual parishes or Diocesan Archives; some microfilmed by FamilySearch but not indexed

## Known record losses

- **Great Pittsburgh Fire (1845):** Destroyed much of downtown Pittsburgh. Some early municipal and business records were lost.
- **1890 federal census:** Approximately 99% destroyed nationwide in a 1921 fire. Substitutes: city directories, tax assessment lists, and state/local records.
- **Company record destruction:** Many steel company records were discarded during corporate mergers and closures in the 20th century. What survives at the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel is the exception, not the rule. Do not assume a company record exists simply because the company was large.

## Research tips

- **Start with the 1880 and 1900 federal censuses.** These are fully indexed, include occupation, and the 1900 census adds immigration year and years in the U.S. — critical for narrowing a port-of-arrival search. ([U.S. Federal Census, Ancestry](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/))
- **City directories are the most practical annual tool.** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds directories from the 1810s. Between census years — especially for the destroyed 1890 census decade — these are the primary means of tracking a Pittsburgh resident year by year. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records))
- **Vital registration began at the county level around 1870 in Allegheny County** and statewide only in 1906. For the 1860s and earlier, and for events missed by county registration, church records are the primary substitute. ([Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))
- **Identify the national parish, not just the religion.** A Slovak Catholic and an Irish Catholic lived in the same city but belonged to different parishes keeping separate registers, often in different languages. The parish register is more useful than the diocese-level search. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records))
- **Naturalization records name the village of origin.** The Declaration of Intention ("first papers") often records the specific town or village in the old country — this is the key to following an immigrant ancestor back to Slovak, Polish, Croatian, or Italian records. Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court; look at the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas first. ([Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records))
- **Pennsylvania is a state-land state.** Original land grants flow from the Pennsylvania Land Office (Harrisburg), not the federal BLM GLO. County deed records at the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds run from 1788. ([Pennsylvania Land and Probate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records))
- **The Allegheny City annexation (1907) is a boundary trap.** If your ancestor lived on the north side of the Allegheny River before 1907, their records are under Allegheny City, not Pittsburgh proper, up to that date.

output.text_response:
Here is the locality guide the research agent assembled for you:

---

# Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic: Records & Repositories

## The core problem: no civil death records exist for 1793

Pennsylvania had no statewide civil death registration until 1906. Every death from the epidemic is documented through **church burial registers, citizen committee records, published death lists, and probate filings** — not government death certificates. That framing shapes everything below.

---

## Epidemic-specific primary sources (start here)

### 1. Mathew Carey's death list
*"A Short Account of the Malignant Fever, Lately Prevalent in Philadelphia"* (1793, multiple editions) includes an appendix naming the dead, compiled from church lists. **This is the fastest first check.** Freely available on the Internet Archive and Google Books. Later editions have longer lists.

### 2. Committee of Citizens records
The citizen relief committee kept minutes and relief lists naming both the sick/dead and the relief workers. Held at the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** and the **Philadelphia City Archives**.

### 3. Bush Hill hospital records
Bush Hill was the fever hospital established during the outbreak. Patient and admission records, to the extent they survive, are at HSP and/or the Philadelphia City Archives.

---

## Church burial registers — the primary mortality record

Because there was no civil registration, church registers are the main death record for 1793. The **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP)** has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church registers.

Key denominations active in 1793 Philadelphia:
- Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church, St. Peter's)
- Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei / Old Swedes')
- German Lutheran and German Reformed
- Quaker (Society of Friends)
- Catholic (St. Mary's)
- Presbyterian
- Baptist, Methodist
- Free African Society (holds its own membership and burial records — central to epidemic relief)

**Most registers are not online** — originals are at HSP, denominational archives, or individual parishes. The GSP index points to these originals.

---

## FamilySearch digitized collections

| Collection | Coverage | Access mode |
|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994 | 3.2 million images; covers 1793 | **Browse-only** (no name index) — navigate to Philadelphia County, 1793–1796 |
| Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 | Indexed + images | Searchable |
| Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 | Indexed, no images | Searchable |
| Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 | 145 images (Quaker admin records) | Browse-only |

**Probate is critical.** The epidemic generated a surge of estate filings in late 1793 and 1794. Probate files name heirs, list assets, and identify minor children and guardians — often the only source for orphaned children whose parents left no other record.

---

## Federal census — bracket the epidemic

- **1790 census** (just before): places households in Philadelphia; indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry
- **1800 census** (after): captures survivors and reconstituted households
- Compare the two: a missing head of household or household with a different structure may signal an epidemic death. Note both censuses name only the head; other members must come from church or court records.

---

## Orphan's Court records

Children orphaned by the epidemic came under court-appointed guardianship. **Philadelphia Orphan's Court petitions, 1793–1795** may be the only record naming a child's parents if the parents left no probate or church record. Held at the Philadelphia City Archives.

---

## Physical repositories

| Repository | Key holdings |
|---|---|
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** | Church records (manuscript + microfilm); Bush Hill hospital records; Committee of Citizens records; private papers |
| **Philadelphia City Archives** | City government records; Committee minutes; Orphan's Court records; deed books |
| **Library Company of Philadelphia** | Early Philadelphia newspapers; Mathew Carey papers; printed primary sources |
| **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP)** | Church record indexes; published transcriptions; Ancestry partnership |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)** | Tax assessment records; some county court records |
| **Denominational archives** | Original Lutheran, Episcopal, Presbyterian, Catholic, Quaker registers |

---

## Newspapers

Philadelphia had active papers in 1793 (*General Advertiser*, *Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser*, others) that published death notices and epidemic lists. On microfilm at HSP and the Library Company. Check **Newspapers.com** and **Chronicling America** for partial digital coverage.

---

## Key research tips

1. **Don't search for a civil death certificate** — none existed in 1793.
2. **Work Orphan's Court records** if children appear to have lost parents; these petitions often name both the deceased parents and the surviving minor children.
3. **The Free African Society records** document the Black community that led much of the relief effort and suffered significant losses. Held at HSP and AME Church archives.
4. **Check neighboring counties.** Thousands fled to Chester, Montgomery, Delaware, and Burlington (NJ) counties during the outbreak. Someone who died while evacuated appears in that county's church records, not Philadelphia's.
5. **Multiple epidemic years.** Philadelphia had additional yellow fever outbreaks in 1797 and 1798. A family may have lost members across more than one season.
6. **Tax assessment records** (Pennsylvania State Archives) can bracket a family's presence in the city when vital records are absent.
7. **Revolutionary War pension files** (Fold3 / NARA): if a veteran pensioner died in 1793, the pension file may document the death and surviving dependents (widow's continuation claim).

---

## What is NOT online

- Committee of Citizens minutes and relief lists
- Bush Hill hospital patient records
- Philadelphia Orphan's Court petitions, 1793–1795
- Most individual Philadelphia church burial registers from 1793
- Philadelphia county assessment/tax lists from the early republic period
- Sexton records for individual cemeteries

These require in-person visits to HSP, the Philadelphia City Archives, or denominational archives.

---

The natural next step is identifying which church served your specific ancestor's neighborhood and denomination, then targeting that register alongside Orphan's Court and probate records for 1793–1795.

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic (c. 1780–1810)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **City and county:** Philadelphia was both a city and a county, with the city proper on the east bank of the Schuylkill River. At the time of the epidemic it was the capital of the United States.
- **Population during the period:** Approximately 50,000 residents in 1793, per the Wikipedia article on the epidemic (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793). `place_population` returned no data for this place and period.
- **Epidemic impact:** Approximately 5,000 deaths — roughly one-tenth of the population — between August and November 1793. Thousands more fled the city temporarily.
- **Economy:** Commercial, governmental, and port city; significant merchant, artisan, and laboring-class populations.
- **Ethnic and religious composition:** English Quakers, German Lutherans and Reformed, Scots-Irish Presbyterians, Anglicans/Episcopalians, Catholics, and a significant free Black community active in epidemic relief through the Free African Society.
- **Key event:** The epidemic itself is the genealogically decisive event — it compressed enormous numbers of deaths, orphanings, property transfers, and estate administrations into a single three-month window.

## Boundary changes

Philadelphia County was established in 1682 and its boundaries were stable during this period. The city and county were legally distinct bodies but coextensive geographically until the Act of Consolidation in 1854. For 1793 research, records could be created at the city level, the county level, or by churches — these are parallel tracks, not substitutes for each other.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until 1906, per the FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968" (collection ID 2255317, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317). There was no civil death registration in force in 1793.
- **What this means for 1793:** All death documentation from the epidemic period is found in church burial registers, institutional records, and published compilations — not in a civil registration system. Do not look for a civil death certificate for a 1793 decedent; none would have been issued.
- **Marriage:** FamilySearch holds "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950" (collection 1571957, 312,045 records, 156,023 images, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) and "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900" (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, index only — no images, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909). These cover the 1793 period and are worth searching for family reconstruction around the epidemic years.

### Church records — PRIMARY SOURCE for 1793 deaths

Church burial registers are the main documentary record of who died during the epidemic. The Wikipedia article on the epidemic names Christ Church, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes'), and other Philadelphia churches as sources of burial records from 1793.

The FamilySearch wiki search result confirms: "burial records from Christ Church, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes'), and other churches" and identifies the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania as having compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church registers. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records

Known denominations present in 1793 Philadelphia:
- Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church, St. Peter's)
- Lutheran and German Reformed
- Quaker (Society of Friends)
- Presbyterian
- Catholic (St. Mary's)
- Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes')
- Methodist
- Baptist

**Where held:** The FamilySearch wiki search result identifies the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Philadelphia City Archives as holding manuscript church records. The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes. Many early Philadelphia church registers have been transcribed and published.

FamilySearch volume_search returned one digitized volume for the Philadelphia area covering 1750-1800: **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes** (image group 001188322, 145 images). This is a Quaker administrative record. It is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only. It is not a burial register but may document members who died and received Quaker relief or care.

**Language:** Records at German Lutheran and German Reformed churches will be in German.

### The Mathew Carey list and Committee records — epidemic-specific primary source

The FamilySearch wiki search result specifically identifies: "the published account by Mathew Carey listing names of the dead" and "minutes and reports of the Committee appointed by the citizens" as key genealogical sources for the 1793 epidemic. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793

Mathew Carey's "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever, Lately Prevalent in Philadelphia" (1793) includes an appendix with names of the dead. This is a published primary source, not a church register — it was compiled from church lists and reports. Multiple editions exist; later editions have longer death lists. It is available through Google Books, the Internet Archive, and many research libraries. This is often the first place to check when you know or suspect someone died in the epidemic.

The Committee of Citizens (sometimes called the Committee to Attend to and Alleviate the Sufferings of the Afflicted) kept minutes and relief lists. These name both the sick/dead and the relief workers. The Wikipedia article and wiki search result both confirm these are held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives.

### Bush Hill hospital records

The wiki search result identifies "records of Bush Hill hospital" as a key genealogical source. Bush Hill was the fever hospital established by the Committee during the epidemic. Its patient and admission records, if surviving, would document the sick and dying. Held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and/or Philadelphia City Archives — the tool results do not specify which portion, if any, has been published or microfilmed.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The 1790 U.S. Federal Census (taken just before the epidemic) places households in Philadelphia and is available online through Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/). The 1800 census captures survivors and reconstituted households. These bracket the epidemic and allow before/after family reconstruction.
- **Digitization level:** The 1790 and 1800 federal censuses are indexed + images on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Note:** The 1790 and 1800 censuses are head-of-household enumerations only — they list all free persons by age and sex bracket but name only the head. Names of other household members must come from other record types.

### Probate and court records

The 1793 epidemic generated a surge of estates and orphan court petitions. Approximately 5,000 deaths in three months meant an enormous volume of probate filings in the months immediately following.

FamilySearch holds "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (collection 1999196, 3,200,560 images, browse-only — 0 indexed records, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196). This covers the 1793 period. Because this is browse-only, you must navigate by county (Philadelphia) and approximate date rather than searching by name. This is a critical source: probate files name heirs, list assets, and often identify minor children and their guardians — useful for tracing orphaned children of epidemic victims.

**Orphan's Court:** Philadelphia's Orphan's Court handled guardianships for children whose parents died. Epidemic orphans from 1793-1794 would appear in Orphan's Court petitions from that period. These are held at the Philadelphia City Archives and at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.

### Land records

Deeds and conveyances at the county recorder of deeds level. Estates sold through probate generated deed transactions in 1793-1795. The FamilySearch wiki page for Pennsylvania generically notes deeds are at county courthouses; for Philadelphia this is the Philadelphia City Archives and the recorder of deeds.

### Military records

The epidemic's direct relevance to military records is limited — it fell between the Revolutionary War (pensions, bounty land) and the War of 1812. Some Philadelphia residents were veterans receiving Revolutionary War pensions in 1793; if a pension holder died in the epidemic, the pension file at NARA (Fold3, https://www.fold3.com/) may document the death and surviving dependents. Widows filed continuation claims when a pensioner died.

### Cemetery records

The epidemic created rapid, high-volume burial demand. Some victims were buried in mass or expedited graves; others in church cemeteries. FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers Philadelphia's historic cemeteries and is worth checking, though transcription coverage for 1793 burials varies by cemetery.

Key Philadelphia cemeteries active in 1793:
- Christ Church Burial Ground
- Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') churchyard
- St. Mary's Catholic cemetery
- Friends (Quaker) burial grounds
- Mikveh Israel (Jewish congregation)

### Newspaper records

Philadelphia had active newspapers in 1793: the General Advertiser (later Aurora), Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser, and others. They published death notices, lists of the dead, and reports on the epidemic. Historical Philadelphia newspapers are held on microfilm at the Library Company of Philadelphia and at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and Chronicling America (Library of Congress) may have partial coverage for this period.

### Immigration/emigration records

NARA holds passenger lists for Philadelphia as a port of entry. Given the epidemic, some families may have emigrated from Philadelphia during or just after the outbreak, or newly arrived immigrants died during it. Passenger lists for the early republic period are available through Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and NARA (https://www.archives.gov/).

### Tax records

Pennsylvania property tax records and county assessment lists exist for Philadelphia for the 1780s-1800s. These can place a family in the city before and after the epidemic. Held at the Pennsylvania State Archives and the Philadelphia City Archives. These are a useful substitute for the non-existent civil vital records of this period.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections / Notes | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 (browse-only images, 3.2M images); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (indexed, no images); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950 (indexed + images); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750-1800 (browse-only, 145 images) | Free |
| Ancestry | 1790 and 1800 U.S. Federal Census (indexed + images); passenger lists | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension files — relevant for veteran deaths in 1793 | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions for Philadelphia's historic burial grounds | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspaper death notices | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Original passenger lists, military records | Free to visit; some digitized |
| Internet Archive / Google Books | Mathew Carey's "Short Account" (1793) — the printed death list from the epidemic | Free |

**Coverage note:** volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for Philadelphia 1780-1810 (the Quaker Yearly Meeting Minutes, 145 images, browse-only). This is a narrow result and is not a complete picture of what FamilySearch has microfilmed — it reflects indexing coverage, not the full microfilm holdings. The FamilySearch Catalog (not queried via API in this run due to tool limitations) is likely to hold additional Philadelphia church register films from this period.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | City government records; Committee of Citizens minutes; Orphan's Court records; deed books | In-person; some materials available via written inquiry |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) | Church records (manuscript and microfilm); Bush Hill hospital records; Committee of Citizens records; private papers of epidemic figures | In-person; advance appointment recommended |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | Early Philadelphia newspapers; Mathew Carey papers; printed primary sources | In-person |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | Tax assessment records; some county court records | In-person; some digitized online |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP) | Indexes to Philadelphia church records; published transcriptions | In-person; some records online via Ancestry partnership |
| Denominational archives | Lutheran, Episcopal, Presbyterian, Catholic, Quaker archives hold original registers | Contact each denomination |

---

## Records NOT online

The following record types exist but have no confirmed online presence based on tool results:

- Committee of Citizens (epidemic relief committee) minutes and relief lists
- Bush Hill hospital patient records
- Philadelphia Orphan's Court guardianship petitions from 1793-1795
- Most individual Philadelphia church burial registers from 1793 (the GSP index points to originals, but the originals themselves are largely at HSP or with the parishes)
- Philadelphia county assessment and tax lists for the early republic period
- Sexton records for individual church cemeteries

---

## Known record losses

No specific courthouse fire or catastrophic loss unique to Philadelphia in this period is confirmed by the tool results. The epidemic itself created record-keeping disruptions: the city government nearly collapsed during the outbreak, and some records from August-November 1793 are incomplete or disorganized. The Wikipedia article notes that "thousands fled the city" — clerks and record-keepers were among them, creating administrative gaps.

---

## Research tips

- **Start with the Mathew Carey death list.** "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793, multiple editions) includes appendices naming the dead compiled from church lists. It is freely available on the Internet Archive and Google Books. It is not comprehensive, but it is the fastest single check. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793

- **Work the 1790 and 1800 censuses as a bracket.** Compare household composition: a head of household who appears in 1790 but whose household in 1800 shows a different head or missing adults may have died in 1793 or in subsequent epidemic years (1797-1798 saw additional outbreaks). Absent children may have been orphaned and placed elsewhere.

- **Church burial registers, not civil death records, are the primary mortality source.** Pennsylvania had no statewide civil death registration in 1793. Every death documentation from the epidemic comes from a church, a committee list, or the Carey publication — there is no government death certificate to find.

- **Probate is essential for tracing epidemic families.** The probate surge of late 1793 and 1794 documents heirs, minors, and estate assets. FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994, browse-only) covers this period. Navigate to Philadelphia County and the 1793-1796 date range and browse.

- **The Free African Society records are a distinct and important source.** The Black community of Philadelphia played a central role in epidemic relief and suffered significant losses. The Free African Society kept its own membership and burial records. These are held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and at the AME Church archives. The FamilySearch wiki search result does not specifically name these, but the Wikipedia epidemic article documents the community's role.

- **Search for orphans in Orphan's Court records.** Children orphaned by the epidemic were placed under court-appointed guardians. Philadelphia Orphan's Court petitions from 1793-1795 at the Philadelphia City Archives may be the only place where a child's parents are named if the parents left no probate or church record.

- **The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP) has compiled church record indexes** for many Philadelphia congregations. Their records are accessible in-person and through a partnership with Ancestry. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records

- **Neighboring jurisdictions matter.** Thousands fled Philadelphia during the epidemic to surrounding Chester, Montgomery, Delaware, and Burlington (NJ) counties. A family member who died while evacuated would appear in that county's church records, not Philadelphia's. If a person cannot be found in Philadelphia records from late 1793, check the rural counties immediately surrounding the city.

- **Multiple epidemic years exist.** The 1793 outbreak was the worst, but Philadelphia experienced additional yellow fever seasons in 1797 and 1798. A family "affected by the epidemic" may have lost members across more than one year.

---

The four `wiki_place_page` sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) all returned a generic fallback page (URL: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Research_Guide) and not Pennsylvania-specific content. The constructed-URL wiki reads for Philadelphia County Genealogy, Pennsylvania Vital Records, Pennsylvania Church Records, and Philadelphia County Vital Records all returned the same generic fallback. No Philadelphia- or Pennsylvania-specific content was available from those pages in this run; all specifics above come from `wiki_search`, `collections_search`, `volume_search`, and the Wikipedia article. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for these topics should be consulted directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy for additional detail not captured here.

---

There is no `research.json` at the working directory, so this guide is presented as standalone Q&A — no locality entry is persisted.

---

Philadelphia in 1793 was the largest city in the new United States, and it kept records through its churches, its courts, and occasionally its civic committees — not through a civil registration system, which Pennsylvania would not create until 1906. When the yellow fever epidemic killed roughly one in ten Philadelphians between August and November 1793, the deaths were documented in church burial registers (Episcopal, Quaker, Lutheran, Catholic, Swedish Lutheran, and others), in the citizen committee's own minutes and relief lists, in the published death lists of Mathew Carey's pamphlet, and in the surge of probate filings that followed. These records are held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania, the Philadelphia City Archives, and the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania, with some digitized images on FamilySearch (particularly probate, which has 3.2 million browse-only images) and the 1790/1800 federal censuses available on Ancestry. Most church registers and committee documents are not online and require in-person visits to Philadelphia repositories.

The natural next step is a focused research plan: identifying which specific churches served your ancestor's neighborhood and denomination, then targeting those registers and the Orphan's Court records for the 1793-1795 window.

Here is the locality guide for Chicago families affected by the Great Fire of 1871:

---

**Locality Survey: Chicago / Cook County, Illinois — ca. 1860–1885**

The Great Chicago Fire (October 8–10, 1871) destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, taking with it virtually all pre-fire civil vital records, deeds, probate files, and court records. That's the central challenge — but substantial sources survive.

---

### What Survived (and Where)

**Census Records**
- **1870 Federal Census** — originals were in Washington, D.C., not Chicago, so they survived intact. This is your primary anchor for households before the fire. Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **1880 Federal Census** — complete; excellent for tracing families after the disaster.
- ⚠️ The 1890 federal census was destroyed in a separate 1921 fire — a second gap to work around.

**Chicago Relief and Aid Society Records**
- Held at the **Chicago History Museum** — arguably the most important source for fire-affected families. These records name displaced households, their pre-fire address, and relief granted. Essential for anyone in Chicago in October 1871.

**Church Records**
- Parishes outside the burn zone survived with their registers intact. Catholic, Lutheran, and other denominations often recorded baptisms, marriages, and burials. The **Newberry Library** and individual diocesan archives hold many of these.

**City Directories**
- The **Newberry Library** holds a near-complete run from the 1840s onward. Because directories were published annually, comparing editions from 1870, 1872, and 1875 can show where a family went after the fire.

**Reconstructed Deed / Property Records**
- The **Burnt Record Act (1872)** authorized reconstruction of pre-fire property records. Reconstructed deed series are held at the **Cook County Recorder of Deeds**.
- **Chicago Title and Trust insurance abstracts** at the Chicago History Museum cover pre-fire property chains.

**FamilySearch Holdings**
- Over **3.3 million indexed Cook County records** beginning in 1871, plus two digitized volumes of reconstructed pre-fire records. Start at [FamilySearch Illinois collections](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/location/1932?region=Illinois).

**Vital Records**
- State registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in Illinois in 1877 — post-fire, so these are intact. Illinois Regional Archives Depositories (IRAD) and the **Illinois State Archives** in Springfield hold them.

---

### Recommended Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Chicago History Museum** | Relief and Aid Society records; insurance abstracts; Chicago Tribune archives |
| **Newberry Library** | City directories; Chicago genealogy collections; church records |
| **Cook County Recorder of Deeds** | Burnt Record Act reconstructed deeds (post-1872) |
| **Illinois State Archives (Springfield)** | Vital records from 1877; military records |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Indexed Cook County records; digitized pre-fire volumes |
| **Illinois Regional Archives Depositories (IRAD)** | County-level civil registration |

---

### Suggested Research Sequence

1. **1870 federal census** — anchor the household before the fire.
2. **Chicago Relief and Aid Society records** — determine if the family appears in the displaced-persons lists.
3. **City directories (1870, 1872, 1875)** — track address changes and survival/relocation.
4. **Church records** — births, marriages, and burials through the fire decade.
5. **1880 federal census** — reconstitute the household a decade later.
6. **Post-1877 vital records** — for events after state registration began.

Many church registers in the fire district also burned in 1871. Parishes outside the northern and western neighborhoods that the fire did not reach may have continuous pre-fire registers. Determine whether your family's parish was in the burn zone before assuming records are gone.
Chicago Title and Trust insurance/property abstracts at the Chicago History Museum partially reconstruct pre-fire property ownership and are not available online.

City directories from the 1840s onward survive at the Newberry Library and are the most reliable annual pre-fire name source. The 1871-72 directory (printed post-fire) documents the reconstituted population.

Civil War pension files at NARA contain neighbor and family affidavits filed in the 1870s-1880s that establish relationships and places of origin independently of destroyed local records — a key workaround for the fire loss.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Cook County (Chicago), Illinois (1860–1885)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County established 1831; Chicago incorporated as a city 1837.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois (state)
- **Economy:** Commerce, meatpacking, grain trading, railroad hub, manufacturing, Great Lakes shipping.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large German, Irish, Scandinavian, and Polish immigrant communities.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (Irish and German parishes), Methodist, Baptist, Lutheran, Presbyterian, Episcopal, Jewish.
- **Key historical events:** Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed roughly 3.3 square miles, killed approximately 300 people, left more than 100,000 homeless, and burned the Cook County Courthouse, destroying most pre-fire civil records.

## Boundary changes
Cook County boundaries were stable throughout this period. The city of Chicago expanded by annexing surrounding townships in stages; the most significant annexation (1889) falls just outside this window.

## The critical fact for this research
The Great Chicago Fire destroyed the Cook County Courthouse on October 8–10, 1871. Lost in the fire were deeds, probate files, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. The 1870 federal census survived because the originals were held in Washington, D.C. The Burnt Record Act of 1872 required property owners to re-register their deeds.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- FamilySearch collections show Cook County civil vital records beginning in 1871 — which aligns with the fire year as the effective start of the surviving county-level series.
- Birth certificates: 1,450,000 records, 1871–1940 (FamilySearch collection id 2024189)
- Death records: 980,000 records, 1871–1947 (FamilySearch collection id 1913456)
- Marriage records: 620,000 records, 1871–1920 (FamilySearch collection id 1756321)
- All pre-October 1871 civil vital records are presumed destroyed.

### Church records
- FamilySearch collection 'Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925' (id 1803978): 285,000 records — indexed + images.
- Archdiocese of Chicago Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic parish registers.
- Many church registers in the fire district also burned. Parishes outside the burn zone may have continuous registers.
- German and Polish parishes kept records in their heritage languages.

### Census records
- 1860, 1870, 1880 federal censuses cover Cook County. The 1870 Chicago census survived because originals were in Washington.
- 1890 federal census destroyed in a separate Washington fire (1921).
- Illinois state censuses: 1855 and 1865 (Illinois State Archives).
- Federal mortality schedules (1860, 1870, 1880) list individuals who died in the year preceding each census.

### Probate and court records
- Pre-fire probate records largely destroyed. Post-fire records from 1871 at IRAD, Northeastern Illinois University.
- FamilySearch: 38 browse-only images of pre-fire reconstructed court records (DGS 009982110, 1865–1871, 0% indexed).
- Post-fire property re-recordings volume (DGS 009982111, 1871–1880): 41% name-indexed.

### Land records
- Illinois is a federal-land state (rectangular survey system).
- Original federal patents: BLM GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov).
- Burnt Record Act of 1872 reconstructed deed series at Cook County Recorder of Deeds.
- Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at Chicago History Museum: insurance-based pre-fire property records.

### Military records
- Civil War service records and pension files: NARA (Fold3, Ancestry).
- Illinois state muster rolls: Illinois State Archives.
- Civil War pension files contain family affidavits — key workaround for fire-destroyed local records.

### Cemetery records
- Major cemeteries: Graceland (1860), Rosehill (1859), Oak Woods, St. Boniface.
- FindAGrave (free): substantial coverage. BillionGraves: some coverage.
- Sexton records at individual cemetery offices.

### Newspaper records
- Chicago Tribune (1847, continuous through fire period); Chicago Times; Illinois Staats-Zeitung (German).
- Tribune published fire-victim relief lists and lists of the displaced in October–December 1871.
- Newspapers.com (subscription); Newberry Library microfilm; Chicago History Museum Tribune archive.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Chicago is inland; most immigrants arrived at East Coast ports (New York/Castle Garden, Baltimore, Quebec) and traveled by rail or Great Lakes vessel.
- Pre-1906 naturalization declarations filed in any court of record — Cook County Circuit Court, U.S. District Court Northern District of Illinois.
- NARA Chicago: naturalization records. Ancestry and FamilySearch: passenger list indices.

### Tax records
- Pre-fire tax rolls destroyed. Post-fire assessment records restart from 1872.
- Cook County Assessor's office; some records at IRAD.
- Useful intercensal substitute given the combined loss of 1871 local records and 1890 federal census.

### Other record types
- City directories (Newberry Library): survive from 1840s onward; essential pre-fire name source.
- Chicago Relief and Aid Society records (Chicago History Museum): named lists of fire-displaced families — one of the most specific post-fire sources.
- Insurance company records: Chicago Title and Trust collection at Chicago History Museum.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Birth Certs 1871–1940 (1.45M); Death Records 1871–1947 (980K); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620K); Church Records 1833–1925 (285K); 2 digitized volumes | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Federal census 1860, 1870, 1880; passenger lists; Civil War records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service records and pension files | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery headstone transcriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Chicago Tribune and other Chicago papers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military pension files, naturalization records | Free finding aids |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Original federal land patents | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Chicago History Museum | Relief and Aid Society records; Chicago Title and Trust records; Tribune archive | In-person; chicagohistory.org |
| Newberry Library | City directories (1840s+); maps; manuscripts | In-person; some digitized |
| IRAD, Northeastern Illinois University | Cook County post-fire civil and court records | In-person; irad.ilsos.gov |
| Archdiocese of Chicago Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers | Written inquiry; archives.archchicago.org |
| Cook County Clerk's Office | Vital records from 1871 | In-person or certified copy |
| Cook County Recorder of Deeds | Burnt Record Act deeds (1872+); post-fire deed books | In-person |
| Illinois State Archives | State census 1855, 1865; Civil War muster rolls | In-person; ilsos.gov |
| NARA Great Lakes (Chicago) | Federal court naturalization records | In-person; nara.gov |

## Records NOT online
- Chicago Relief and Aid Society recipient records (Chicago History Museum)
- Chicago Title and Trust insurance/property abstracts (Chicago History Museum)
- Most pre-fire church registers that survived (individual parishes or diocesan archives)
- Cook County Assessor post-fire tax records (IRAD)
- Illinois state census schedules 1855, 1865 (Illinois State Archives)
- Sexton records for individual Chicago cemeteries

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Cook County (Chicago), Illinois (1860–1885)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County established 1831; Chicago incorporated as a city 1837.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois (state)
- **Economy:** Commerce, meatpacking, grain trading, railroad hub, manufacturing, Great Lakes shipping.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large German, Irish, Scandinavian, and Polish immigrant communities.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (Irish and German parishes), Methodist, Baptist, Lutheran, Presbyterian, Episcopal, Jewish.
- **Key historical events:** Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed roughly 3.3 square miles, killed approximately 300 people, left more than 100,000 homeless, and burned the Cook County Courthouse, destroying most pre-fire civil records.

## Boundary changes
Cook County boundaries were stable throughout this period. The city of Chicago expanded by annexing surrounding townships in stages; the most significant annexation (1889) falls just outside this window.

## The critical fact for this research
The Great Chicago Fire destroyed the Cook County Courthouse on October 8–10, 1871. Lost in the fire were deeds, probate files, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. The 1870 federal census survived because the originals were held in Washington, D.C. The Burnt Record Act of 1872 required property owners to re-register their deeds.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- FamilySearch collections show Cook County civil vital records beginning in 1871 — which aligns with the fire year as the effective start of the surviving county-level series.
- Birth certificates: 1,450,000 records, 1871–1940 (FamilySearch collection id 2024189)
- Death records: 980,000 records, 1871–1947 (FamilySearch collection id 1913456)
- Marriage records: 620,000 records, 1871–1920 (FamilySearch collection id 1756321)
- All pre-October 1871 civil vital records are presumed destroyed.

### Church records
- FamilySearch collection 'Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925' (id 1803978): 285,000 records — indexed + images.
- Archdiocese of Chicago Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic parish registers.
- Many church registers in the fire district also burned. Parishes outside the burn zone may have continuous registers.
- German and Polish parishes kept records in their heritage languages.

### Census records
- 1860, 1870, 1880 federal censuses cover Cook County. The 1870 Chicago census survived because originals were in Washington.
- 1890 federal census destroyed in a separate Washington fire (1921).
- Illinois state censuses: 1855 and 1865 (Illinois State Archives).
- Federal mortality schedules (1860, 1870, 1880) list individuals who died in the year preceding each census.

### Probate and court records
- Pre-fire probate records largely destroyed. Post-fire records from 1871 at IRAD, Northeastern Illinois University.
- FamilySearch: 38 browse-only images of pre-fire reconstructed court records (DGS 009982110, 1865–1871, 0% indexed).
- Post-fire property re-recordings volume (DGS 009982111, 1871–1880): 41% name-indexed.

### Land records
- Illinois is a federal-land state (rectangular survey system).
- Original federal patents: BLM GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov).
- Burnt Record Act of 1872 reconstructed deed series at Cook County Recorder of Deeds.
- Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at Chicago History Museum: insurance-based pre-fire property records.

### Military records
- Civil War service records and pension files: NARA (Fold3, Ancestry).
- Illinois state muster rolls: Illinois State Archives.
- Civil War pension files contain family affidavits — key workaround for fire-destroyed local records.

### Cemetery records
- Major cemeteries: Graceland (1860), Rosehill (1859), Oak Woods, St. Boniface.
- FindAGrave (free): substantial coverage. BillionGraves: some coverage.
- Sexton records at individual cemetery offices.

### Newspaper records
- Chicago Tribune (1847, continuous through fire period); Chicago Times; Illinois Staats-Zeitung (German).
- Tribune published fire-victim relief lists and lists of the displaced in October–December 1871.
- Newspapers.com (subscription); Newberry Library microfilm; Chicago History Museum Tribune archive.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Chicago is inland; most immigrants arrived at East Coast ports (New York/Castle Garden, Baltimore, Quebec) and traveled by rail or Great Lakes vessel.
- Pre-1906 naturalization declarations filed in any court of record — Cook County Circuit Court, U.S. District Court Northern District of Illinois.
- NARA Chicago: naturalization records. Ancestry and FamilySearch: passenger list indices.

### Tax records
- Pre-fire tax rolls destroyed. Post-fire assessment records restart from 1872.
- Cook County Assessor's office; some records at IRAD.
- Useful intercensal substitute given the combined loss of 1871 local records and 1890 federal census.

### Other record types
- City directories (Newberry Library): survive from 1840s onward; essential pre-fire name source.
- Chicago Relief and Aid Society records (Chicago History Museum): named lists of fire-displaced families — one of the most specific post-fire sources.
- Insurance company records: Chicago Title and Trust collection at Chicago History Museum.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Birth Certs 1871–1940 (1.45M); Death Records 1871–1947 (980K); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620K); Church Records 1833–1925 (285K); 2 digitized volumes | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Federal census 1860, 1870, 1880; passenger lists; Civil War records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service records and pension files | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery headstone transcriptions | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Chicago Tribune and other Chicago papers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military pension files, naturalization records | Free finding aids |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Original federal land patents | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Chicago History Museum | Relief and Aid Society records; Chicago Title and Trust records; Tribune archive | In-person; chicagohistory.org |
| Newberry Library | City directories (1840s+); maps; manuscripts | In-person; some digitized |
| IRAD, Northeastern Illinois University | Cook County post-fire civil and court records | In-person; irad.ilsos.gov |
| Archdiocese of Chicago Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers | Written inquiry; archives.archchicago.org |
| Cook County Clerk's Office | Vital records from 1871 | In-person or certified copy |
| Cook County Recorder of Deeds | Burnt Record Act deeds (1872+); post-fire deed books | In-person |
| Illinois State Archives | State census 1855, 1865; Civil War muster rolls | In-person; ilsos.gov |
| NARA Great Lakes (Chicago) | Federal court naturalization records | In-person; nara.gov |

## Records NOT online
- Chicago Relief and Aid Society recipient records (Chicago History Museum)
- Chicago Title and Trust insurance/property abstracts (Chicago History Museum)
- Most pre-fire church registers that survived (individual parishes or diocesan archives)
- Cook County Assessor post-fire tax records (IRAD)
- Illinois state census schedules 1855, 1865 (Illinois State Archives)
- Sexton records for individual Chicago cemeteries

## Known record losses
| Loss | Date | What was lost | Substitutes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cook County Courthouse fire | October 1871 | Pre-fire deeds, probate, vital records, court records, tax rolls | Burnt Record Act deeds; Chicago Title and Trust; church registers; city directories; 1870 federal census |
| Many Chicago church registers | October 1871 | Baptism, marriage, burial registers in fire district | Diocesan archives; registers for parishes outside burn zone |
| 1890 federal census | 1921 | Entire U.S. 1890 census | City directories, tax records, state records |

## Research tips
- Start with the 1870 federal census — it survived and is the most complete pre-fire household record.
- Search Tribune relief lists (October–December 1871) on Newspapers.com or at the Chicago History Museum before assuming a family cannot be traced.
- The Chicago Relief and Aid Society records at the Chicago History Museum list displaced households by name — treat as a substitute census for late 1871.
- Reconstruct property through the Burnt Record Act: the reconstructed deed often recites the full chain of title back to the original federal patent.
- Civil War pension files at NARA contain neighbor and family affidavits from the 1870s–1880s — a key workaround for fire-destroyed local records.
- Consult familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Genealogy directly; the wiki_place_page sections returned a generic fallback rather than an Illinois-specific article.

Here is what the locality-guide agent found:

---

## Louisiana French Colonial Period (1699–1769): Research Guide

### Jurisdiction Overview
The French colonial period runs roughly **1699–1769**, ending when Spain took effective administrative control under O'Reilly. New Orleans (founded 1718) was the capital. The colony followed Roman Catholic practice exclusively (Code Noir), with Capuchin and Jesuit clergy administering parishes.

**Critical periodization note:** The 1762–1769 transition (France ceding to Spain) is genealogically fuzzy — records may follow French or Spanish administrative forms depending on locality. Treat 1762–1800 as one continuous research era requiring both languages.

---

### Key Record Types

**1. Catholic Parish Registers (THE vital register)**
Civil registration didn't exist — the Church was the de facto registrar. Registers record baptisms, marriages, and burials, including enslaved persons (required by Code Noir).
- **FamilySearch collection 1612905** — *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925* (~987,654 records, images)
- **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** — holds originals from 1720
- Two digitized FamilySearch volumes (browse-only, not name-indexed, in French/Spanish): 264 images of Orleans sacramental registers, 1720–1803
- **Gap warning:** Outlying posts (Natchitoches, Pointe Coupee, Natchez) have incomplete registers

**2. Superior Council Records (court + notary in one)**
The colony's governing and judicial body handled land grants, estate inventories, contracts, slave sales, criminal proceedings — everything you'd search in both a courthouse and deed book elsewhere.
- FamilySearch has one volume (004330992): 149 images, 1699–1769, **browse-only, French, not indexed**
- **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) holds the primary archive

**3. New Orleans Notarial Archives**
The oldest continuous notarial office in North America (records from the 1730s): marriage contracts (naming parents on both sides), wills, manumissions, property transactions, apprenticeships. Often the richest source for family relationships.

**4. French National Archives (ANOM — Aix-en-Provence, France)**
This is the most overlooked repository. Holds:
- Colonial census rolls (nominative lists naming individuals)
- Emigrant/passenger lists (including the 1717–1731 Company of the Indies transports)
- Military rosters (Compagnies Franches de la Marine)
- Administrative correspondence
- Access: In-person or via ANOM's online portal (anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr)

**5. Probate/Estate Records**
- FamilySearch collection 2078341 — *Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984* (overlaps late French and Spanish colonial periods)
- Louisiana civil law (not common law): wills were notarized, not court-filed; estates went through the Superior Council

**6. Land Records (French Long-Lot System)**
- Concessions recorded in Superior Council records and notarial archives
- American State Papers: Public Lands confirms colonial grants post-1803
- Key: arpent measurements, not the rectangular US survey grid

---

### Repository Summary

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collections 1612905 & 2078341; 2 digitized volumes (413 images total, browse-only) | Free online |
| Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans | Superior Council records (primary colonial archive) | In-person |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives | Notarial acts from 1730s | In-person |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Original parish registers from 1720 | Written inquiry or in-person |
| **ANOM, Aix-en-Provence, France** | Census rolls, emigrant lists, military records — most of the administrative record | In-person or online portal |

---

### Practical Research Tips

1. **Start with the church registers.** FamilySearch collection 1612905 first, then contact the Archdiocese for anything not digitized.
2. **The two FamilySearch digitized volumes are browse-only** — no name index, must be read image by image. French paleography skills are required.
3. **Don't skip ANOM.** Most American genealogists overlook French national archives, but colonial census rolls and emigrant lists are there, not in Louisiana.
4. **For enslaved ancestors:** The Code Noir mandated Catholic baptism — parish registers are the primary source. Notarial records hold manumissions and sale documents naming individuals.
5. **Identify the specific post first** (New Orleans, Natchitoches, German Coast, Pointe Coupee, etc.) — records are organized geographically, not by a single statewide index.
6. **Check published transcriptions** before traveling. Winston De Ville (colonial census abstracts) and Glenn Conrad (passenger lists, church record abstracts) have put significant material into print, available at large genealogical libraries via WorldCat.

---

**Bottom line:** The overwhelming majority of French colonial Louisiana records are NOT name-indexed online. The two FamilySearch digitized volumes total only 413 browse-only images. Serious research requires contacting physical repositories in New Orleans and, for administrative records, France.
