# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1699–1769)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** The colony of French Louisiana was claimed by France in 1682 (La Salle's Mississippi River expedition). The permanent colonial administration took effective hold from 1699 onward. New Orleans was founded in 1718 and became the colonial capital.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (founded 1718); post at Mobile (1702) preceded it
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of New France, administered from France; Superior Council (Conseil Superieur) held local authority
- **Population during period:** No reliable tool data returned for colonial-era figures. Per Wikipedia: sparse European settlement in the early decades, growing with the Company of the Indies (1717-1731) and subsequent royal control. The colony was never densely populated.
- **Economy:** Tobacco, indigo, furs, lumber, later sugarcane; river trade along the Mississippi. Enslaved labor under the Code Noir.
- **Ethnic composition:** French settlers (including Canadians/Canadiens), German Coast settlers (Germans recruited 1720s), African enslaved people (predominantly from Senegambia), free people of color, small numbers of Indigenous allies
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively under French colonial law; the Code Noir prohibited other religions and required Catholic baptism of enslaved persons. The Capuchins and Jesuits administered parishes.
- **Key historical events:** 1699 Iberville establishes first settlement; 1718 New Orleans founded; 1722 hurricane destroys early New Orleans; 1729 Natchez massacre; 1731 Crown takes colony from Company of the Indies; 1762 Treaty of Fontainebleau (France secretly cedes west bank to Spain); 1769 Spain takes effective control under O'Reilly — this is the end of the primary French colonial administrative record era.

**Note on periodization:** The 1700s span two distinct colonial regimes. The French colonial period (1699–1769) and the Spanish colonial period (1769–1803) each produced their own record series, often in different languages and through different administrative structures. This guide focuses on the French period. Records from 1769 onward are predominantly Spanish colonial records (in Spanish, held in the same Louisiana repositories).

## Boundary changes

- **1699–1762:** French Louisiana was a single administrative unit covering the Mississippi River basin. The colony had no counties in the English sense; it was organized into discrete posts and parishes.
- **1762 (Treaty of Fontainebleau):** France secretly ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain. The eastern bank (between the Mississippi and the Perdido River) went to Britain in 1763 (Treaty of Paris). This split the territory, but Spain did not assume effective administrative control until 1769 — records for 1762–1769 remain largely under French administrative form even as sovereignty changed.
- **1769:** Spanish administration begins. Records transition from French-language Superior Council instruments to Spanish-language cabildo records. Genealogically, these are a continuous record stream despite the political rupture.
- A record created in, say, the Natchitoches district in 1750 was a French colonial record; one from the same place in 1780 is a Spanish colonial record. Both are now held in the same Louisiana repositories.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Civil registration did not exist in French Louisiana. There was no government requirement for civil birth, marriage, or death registration during the colonial period.
- **What exists:** The Catholic Church was the de facto registrar. Parish registers (sacramental records) record baptisms, marriages, and burials. The FamilySearch collection **Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925** (collection ID 1612905) covers this period. It contains approximately 987,654 records with image access.
- **Where held:** The Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives holds original registers. FamilySearch has digitized volumes: 2 volumes were returned by volume_search, both browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable), in French and Spanish. The St. Louis Cathedral registers from 1720 are a key source per the wiki_search result ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)).
- **Gaps:** Outlying settlements (Natchitoches, Pointe Coupee, Natchez before 1729) had intermittent priest coverage; registers are incomplete or missing for many posts.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Notarial records (marriage contracts), Superior Council proceedings (estate inventories naming heirs), and military muster rolls.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only (legally exclusive under French colonial law). Capuchin friars served New Orleans and lower Louisiana; Jesuits served upper Louisiana and Illinois Country (ceded as a separate district). No Protestant churches were permitted.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including enslaved persons, as required by the Code Noir), marriages (often preceded by civil marriage contracts drawn before a notary), and burials. Confirmations are a separate dated event and appear in some registers.
- **Accessible digitized volumes (from volume_search):**
  - **Volume 004330991** — Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans; 264 images; coverage 1720–1803, Orleans parish; 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; in French and Spanish. **Browse-only images.**
  - These are the only 2 volumes returned in the entire volume_search result (totalResults: 2). This represents a significant digitization gap for outlying colonial parishes.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives (in-person or written inquiry). FamilySearch collection 1612905 (online, browse-only for colonial-era material). The Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans) also holds some sacramental materials.
- **Language:** French for the period 1699–1769; mixture of French and Spanish thereafter. Researchers must be able to read 18th-century French script.

### Superior Council (Conseil Superieur) Records

This is the most important non-church record series for French colonial Louisiana and has no direct parallel in later American records.

- **What exists:** The Superior Council was the colony's governing and judicial body. Its records include: land concessions (grants), contracts, court proceedings, estate inventories and successions, slave sale documents, debt cases, criminal proceedings, and administrative correspondence.
- **Accessible digitized volumes (from volume_search):**
  - **Volume 004330992** — French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records); 149 images; coverage 1699–1769, Louisiana; 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; in French. **Browse-only images.**
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans — holds the primary Superior Council archive and has partially digitized it, per the wiki_search result ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)). FamilySearch Probate Records collection (ID 2078341, date range 1756–1984) overlaps the late colonial period.
- **Language:** French. 18th-century notarial French script is specialized; consider consulting a paleographer.

### Census records

- **Colonial censuses:** France took periodic census rolls of the Louisiana colony. The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France holds administrative correspondence and census rolls for the colony, per the wiki_search result ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)). These are nominative lists (listing individuals by name) for some years.
- **Federal census:** Louisiana joined the US in 1803. The first federal census covering Louisiana is 1810. This postdates the French colonial period entirely.
- **Access:** ANOM census rolls are held physically in France; some have been microfilmed and may be accessible via interlibrary loan or digital surrogates through French archival portals (e.g., ANOM's own online interface at anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr).

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Estate inventories, successions, guardianships — all processed through the Superior Council during the French period, not through separate probate courts as in common-law jurisdictions. Louisiana follows civil law tradition (derived from French and Spanish law), so probate practice differs from that in American common-law states.
- **Date range:** From earliest settlement; the FamilySearch collection **Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984** (collection ID 2078341) overlaps the late French and Spanish colonial periods.
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center (Superior Council archives); some digitized in FamilySearch collection 2078341. Civil law estate records continue through the Spanish period in the same repositories.
- **Note on testate vs. intestate:** French civil law (and its Louisiana successor) treats succession differently from common-law probate. Wills (testaments) were notarized, not filed with a court at death; intestate successions were administered through the Superior Council. Search both the notarial archives and the Superior Council records regardless of whether the ancestor left a will.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** French long lots (arpent system) — narrow strips perpendicular to waterways, not the rectangular survey grid used elsewhere in the US. Understanding this system is essential to locating the correct land records.
- **Land distribution:** French concessions (grants) were issued by the Superior Council and the Company of the Indies. These were recorded in the Superior Council records, not in a separate land office.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Land Office (post-1803 American patents); **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** for colonial-era notarial transactions from the 1730s onward, per wiki_search result ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)). American State Papers: Public Lands series documents colonial grants that were confirmed after the Louisiana Purchase.
- **Note:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives is the oldest continuous notarial office in North America. Its holdings begin in the 1730s and include marriage contracts, property transactions, wills, and contracts — a major genealogical resource for the colonial period that is separate from the Superior Council records.

### Military records

- **Relevant period:** Ongoing French-British and French-Indigenous conflicts throughout the 1700s; the Natchez War (1729), King George's War (1740s), Seven Years' War/French and Indian War (1754–1763).
- **Record types:** Company rosters and muster rolls for the Compagnies Franches de la Marine (the colonial troops). Pension records are minimal in the colonial context.
- **Where held:** ANOM (Aix-en-Provence, France) holds the bulk of French colonial military records. Some have been filmed; access is primarily through the French national archive system. NARA holds post-1803 military records only.

### Cemetery records

- **Context:** Formal cemetery records in the modern sense did not exist during the French colonial period. Burials were recorded in church burial registers (see Church Records above).
- **Major sites:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 in New Orleans (established 1789, at the end of the Spanish period); earlier colonial burials may have been on church grounds that no longer survive.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has some listings, but colonial-era coverage is sparse.

### Newspaper records

- **Colonial-era:** No newspapers were published in French Louisiana during the colonial period. The first Louisiana newspaper, the Moniteur de la Louisiane, did not appear until 1794 (Spanish period).
- **Not applicable** as a primary source for the 1700s French colonial period.

### Immigration / emigration records

- **Relevant sources:** Lists of colonists sent to Louisiana by the Company of the Indies (1717–1731) survive in French archives. Passenger lists for ships arriving at New Orleans during the colonial period are in ANOM and have been partially published (e.g., Glenn Conrad's published guides).
- **Engages (indentured workers) and forced deportees:** Records of the "correction" transports of 1717–1721 (criminals and undesirables sent to build the colony) survive in French archives.
- **Where held:** ANOM, Aix-en-Provence. Some published transcriptions are available at the Louisiana Historical Center and in print at research libraries.
- **Post-1803:** Passenger lists at NARA cover the American period only.

### Tax records

- **Colonial period:** Formal property tax rolls in the American sense did not exist under French colonial administration. The Superior Council records include some assessment-related documents. Spanish colonial capitation and property records begin after 1769.
- **Substitute value:** The colonial census rolls (see Census records) partially substitute by listing heads of household and property.

### Other record types

- **Notarial archives:** Covered under Land Records above, but worth emphasizing separately. The New Orleans Notarial Archives holds French-language notarial acts from the 1730s: marriage contracts, apprenticeship agreements, business contracts, manumissions of enslaved people, and wills. This is often the richest source for family relationships in the colonial period.
- **Code Noir records:** The Code Noir (1724 Louisiana version) required baptism, marriage, and burial of enslaved persons in the Catholic Church. Sacramental registers are therefore a primary source for enslaved ancestors in French Louisiana. Manumission documents (affranchissements) appear in notarial records.
- **Slave sale documents:** Recorded in notarial and Superior Council records; name enslaved persons and sometimes their origins.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (ID 1612905; ~987,654 records, images); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (ID 2078341; ~456,789 records, images) | Free |
| FamilySearch (digitized volumes) | Vol. 004330991: Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans, 1720–1803 (264 images, browse-only, French/Spanish); Vol. 004330992: French colonial notarial acts / Superior Council, 1699–1769 (149 images, browse-only, French) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census (post-1803 only; not relevant to French colonial period) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Post-1803 American records only for Louisiana | Free to search; fees for copies |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery listings (sparse for colonial period) | Free |

**Coverage note:** The volume_search returned a total of 2 digitized volumes matching Louisiana for 1700–1800. These are the complete result set (no further pages). This is a very small digitized footprint for the colonial period — the overwhelming majority of French colonial Louisiana records remain either in physical repositories or in French national archives (ANOM) not yet fully integrated into FamilySearch or Ancestry.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans | Superior Council records (primary French colonial court/notarial archive), partially digitized; sacramental record copies | In-person; contact for research inquiries |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center, New Orleans | Notarial acts from 1730s onward (marriage contracts, property transactions, wills); oldest continuous notarial office in North America | In-person; some records on microfilm |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Original Catholic parish registers, 1720 onward; pre-1720 fragments | Written inquiry or in-person |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative correspondence, census rolls, military records, emigrant lists; the central archive for French colonial Louisiana | In-person (Aix-en-Provence) or via ANOM's online portal and microfilm orders |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Post-territorial records; some colonial-era transferred materials | In-person; some online access |
| Louisiana State University Special Collections, Baton Rouge | Published guides, transcribed records, colonial-era maps | In-person; some digitized |

---

## Records NOT online

The following exist but are not available through any online name-searchable database:

- The majority of French colonial Catholic sacramental registers outside New Orleans (Natchitoches, Pointe Coupee, Attakapas, Illinois Country)
- Colonial census rolls (nominative lists held at ANOM)
- French colonial military rosters and pension-related documents (at ANOM)
- Emigrant/passenger lists from colonial-era ships (at ANOM; some published in print)
- The bulk of Superior Council proceedings beyond the 149-image FamilySearch volume
- Notarial acts outside New Orleans for outlying colonial posts

---

## Known record losses

- The 1788 and 1794 New Orleans fires destroyed a portion of the city's early built environment, though the main archival repositories (church and notarial) survived in large part because they were dispersed or protected.
- Records for many outlying posts (Natchez, Biloxi, Mobile) are fragmentary or lost due to military conflict, abandonment, or transfer to other jurisdictions when boundaries changed.
- Britain received the eastern bank of the Mississippi in 1763; records from posts in that territory may have been carried to British Florida archives or are now at the Public Record Office / The National Archives (UK) rather than in Louisiana repositories.

---

## Research tips

- **The Church is the vital register.** There was no civil registration in French Louisiana. The Catholic parish register is the birth/marriage/death record for this period. Begin every family search at FamilySearch collection 1612905 and the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives. ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))
- **The Superior Council is the court AND the notary.** In common-law states, you search the court separately from the deed book. In French Louisiana, the Superior Council handled land grants, estate inventories, contracts, and civil disputes all in one archive. Think of it as the courthouse and the notary's office combined. ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))
- **Go to France for colonial-era administrative records.** The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence is the single most important repository for French colonial Louisiana that most American genealogists overlook. Census rolls, emigrant lists, military rosters, and administrative correspondence are there. ANOM has an online catalog and some digitized holdings accessible at their website. ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))
- **The notarial archive is a genealogical goldmine.** The New Orleans Notarial Archives holds marriage contracts (often drawn before the church marriage and naming parents on both sides), manumissions, apprenticeships, and wills from the 1730s. This is often the richest source for family relationships, particularly for free people of color and merchant families. ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))
- **Records in French require 18th-century French paleography skills.** The two FamilySearch digitized volumes are in French (and Spanish for post-1769 material). Neither is name-indexed; both must be browsed image by image. Standard typing searches will not find colonial-era individuals.
- **The Code Noir requires searching enslaved ancestors in church registers.** French colonial law mandated Catholic baptism of all enslaved people; the registers record their names (sometimes African-origin names), sometimes their nation of origin, and their enslaver's name. This is the primary documentary source for enslaved ancestors in French Louisiana.
- **Track the jurisdictional split of 1762–1769.** During the transition period (France ceding to Spain), some records appear under French administrative forms, others begin the Spanish series. Treat 1762–1800 as a single research era requiring knowledge of both French and Spanish record-keeping conventions.
- **The long-lot survey system means land records use arpent measurements.** When reading land descriptions in the Superior Council or notarial records, arpents (French units) describe narrow strips along bayous and rivers. A genealogical atlas of Louisiana's colonial settlements is essential for geographic orientation.
- **Published transcriptions exist for some series.** The work of researchers like Winston De Ville (colonial census transcriptions) and Glenn Conrad (passenger lists, church record abstracts) has put some colonial records into print. Check large genealogical libraries and WorldCat before booking a trip to France or New Orleans.

---

**Massachusetts, 1620–1700 — Puritan-Era Locality Guide**

This survey covers both **Plymouth Colony** and **Massachusetts Bay Colony** for the Puritan settlement period. Records from this era are among the richest in colonial North America. Key points before you start:

**Civil Vital Records (Town Level)**
Massachusetts required towns to register births, marriages, and deaths beginning in **1639** — at the *town* level, not statewide. Town clerk records are your primary civil vital record source. Before 1639, and as a parallel source throughout the period, **Congregational church records** are essential.

**Key Record Types & Repositories**

- **Town vital records** — FamilySearch holds an indexed collection covering this period with millions of records.
- **Church records** — Congregational (Puritan) parish registers of births/baptisms, marriages, and burials. FamilySearch has indexed these alongside two browse-only digitized volumes of colonial-era church admissions.
- **Probate records** — FamilySearch's indexed colonial-era probate collection is a major source for family relationships, property, and household composition.
- **Proprietors' records** — Digitized volumes on FamilySearch (browse-only) covering land grants and town proprietors.
- **The Great Migration Study** — Published by **NEHGS (New England Historic Genealogical Society)** in Boston, this multi-volume series is indispensable for any ancestor who arrived before **1643**. It is the gold standard for early Massachusetts families not yet fully represented in searchable online databases.

**Important Context**
- The **two-colony split** (Plymouth vs. Massachusetts Bay) matters for jurisdiction — records were kept separately until the 1691 merger into the Province of Massachusetts Bay.
- England (and its colonies) used the **Julian calendar** until 1752. Dates between January 1 and March 24 in this era may be written in Old Style (e.g., "1 February 1648/9") — you'll need to account for this when reading and citing dates.

**Next Step**
If you want to move from this survey into a research plan for a specific ancestor, that would be the next step.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620-1700) — Early Puritan Settlement Period

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Plymouth Colony established 1620; Massachusetts Bay Colony chartered 1628, settlers arrived 1630. Merged into Province of Massachusetts Bay 1691.
- **Administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown / Council for New England (pre-1691)
- **Economy:** Subsistence and commercial agriculture, fishing, lumber, fur trade, small-scale manufacturing
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; indentured servants; small number of enslaved people by mid-century; indigenous Algonquian peoples throughout
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) established church; persecuted Quakers; small numbers of Anglicans and Baptists toward century's end
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration 1630-1640; Antinomian Controversy 1636-1638; Pequot War 1636-1637; King Philip's War 1675-1676 (record losses); Salem witch trials 1692; 1691 merger of Plymouth and Massachusetts Bay

## Boundary changes
- 1620-1691: Two separate jurisdictions — Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony — with separate records
- 1691: Province of Massachusetts Bay absorbs Plymouth Colony
- Counties established within Massachusetts Bay 1643 (Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk, Suffolk); before 1643 the General Court handled colony-wide matters
- King Philip's War 1675-1676 destroyed records in frontier towns

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- Town-level registration mandated from 1639 (not county or statewide)
- Statewide civil registration did not begin until 1842
- FamilySearch collection: Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (ID 2061550, ~3.4M records)
- Published abstracts: Tanner-Corbin 'Vital Records of [Town] to 1850' series covers 200+ towns
- Pre-1639: no civil vital records — Congregational church records only

### Church records
- Congregational (Puritan) is dominant; membership lists, baptisms, marriages, disciplinary proceedings, burials
- FamilySearch collection: Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (ID 1921657, ~987K records)
- Browse-only digitized volume: Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms, 1630-1700 (imageGroupNumber 007612045, 121 images, full-text searchable, 0% name-indexed)
- Congregational Library & Archives and NEHGS hold major manuscript collections

### Census records
- No federal census before 1790 — entirely outside this period
- Colony-era musters and tax assessments at Massachusetts Archives
- Town proprietors' records function as household enumeration for early settlers
- Browse-only digitized volume: Massachusetts town meeting and proprietors' records 1620-1698 (imageGroupNumber 007612044, 188 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable)

### Probate and court records
- FamilySearch collection: Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (ID 1678901, ~567K records)
- County probate from 1643; General Court handled probate before that
- Plymouth Colony court records published separately in 'Records of the Colony of New Plymouth'

### Land records
- Metes and bounds survey system
- Initial grants by General Court and town proprietors' committees; subsequent transfers at county registries of deeds from 1643
- County Registries of Deeds hold originals; Massachusetts Archives holds colony grants

### Military records
- Pequot War 1636-1637; King Philip's War 1675-1676
- Muster rolls, militia lists at Massachusetts Archives; published in Colonial Society of Massachusetts series
- No NARA federal records for this period

### Cemetery records
- Colonial burying grounds in Boston (King's Chapel 1630, Granary 1660, Copp's Hill 1659), Salem, Plymouth, Cambridge, Ipswich
- FindAGrave has transcriptions; early stones often worn beyond legibility

### Newspapers
- No ongoing colonial newspaper for 1620-1700 period

output.text_response:
Here is the locality-guide agent's full response:

---

**Locality entry written as `loc_001`.**

---

## Key Findings: Alabama Before Statehood (~1800)

### ⚠️ Critical Flags Up Front

**The digitization gap is real and significant.** FamilySearch's volume search returned **zero browsable image volumes** for Alabama in the pre-statehood period — in both a restricted query (1780–1820) and an unrestricted one. The four indexed FamilySearch collections all begin in 1803 or later, and their pre-1819 coverage is partial. This is not a sign that records don't exist — it means surviving records are **physical holdings** scattered across ADAH, MDAH, NARA, the Archdiocese of Mobile, and European colonial archives. For this period, **you cannot research entirely online.**

**The most consequential quirk is the dual-sovereignty split around Mobile.** Around 1800, Alabama was not one record-keeping jurisdiction — it was at least two operating simultaneously and independently:
- The **American Mississippi Territory** (covering the interior)
- The **Spanish Mobile District** (covering the coastal zone)

Searching the wrong system produces a true negative that means nothing. You need to pin down *where* within the region your ancestor lived before choosing which archival chain to search.

---

## Jurisdictional Context

| Year | Event |
|------|-------|
| 1795 | Pinckney's Treaty — Spain cedes most of present-day Alabama to the U.S. |
| 1798 | **Mississippi Territory** created (included most of present Alabama) |
| 1800s | Mobile and coastal strip remain under Spanish control |
| 1813 | U.S. forces seize Mobile — Spanish era ends in Alabama |
| 1817 | Alabama Territory separated from Mississippi Territory |
| 1819 | **Alabama achieves statehood** |

Counties existing in the pre-statehood window:
- **Washington County** (1800) — first organized county in Alabama
- **Madison County** (1808) — Tennessee Valley area
- **Baldwin and Mobile counties** (1809) — coastal zone, formerly Spanish

---

## Record Types and Where They Are Held

### Land Records
- **Most accessible pre-statehood source.** U.S. land patents from the Mississippi Territory period are searchable via the **BLM General Land Office Records** (glorecords.blm.gov), many digitized.
- Spanish land grants (coastal zone) are held by **ADAH** and the **AGI in Seville** (Archivo General de Indias).
- Federal land entry case files: **NARA (Washington, D.C.)** — not yet widely digitized.

### Territorial Census / Population Schedules
- **1800 U.S. Federal Census** covers Washington County (part of Mississippi Territory). This *is* indexed and searchable.
- **1810 U.S. Federal Census** covers Madison, Washington, and other early counties.
- FamilySearch collections: *Alabama, Early American Series, 1820–1969* and *Alabama Census Records* — both start post-statehood for the most part.

### Vital Records (Birth, Marriage, Death)
- **No civil registration before statehood.** State-mandated vital records don't begin until the late 19th century.
- **Church records** are the primary source: Catholic parish registers from Mobile (Spanish era), Methodist circuit records, Baptist church minutes.
- **Mobile Archdiocese** holds Spanish-era Catholic registers. Some are microfilmed; FamilySearch has partial holdings beginning around 1704 for Mobile.

### Probate and Court Records
- Washington County probate and court records from 1800 onward survive at **ADAH** and the county courthouse; some are microfilmed by FamilySearch but the pre-1820 window is sparse online.
- Mississippi Territory superior court records: **MDAH** (Mississippi Department of Archives and History), since the territory was administered from Natchez.

### Military Records
- **War of 1812 service records and pension files** — NARA; Fold3 has digitized many.
- Territorial militia musters: scattered, held at ADAH.

### Spanish Colonial Records (Mobile District, pre-1813)
- Census lists (*padrones*), notarial records, land grants, church registers — primarily at **AGI Seville** and **ADAH**.
- The **Papeles Procedentes de Cuba** series at AGI is the richest source for the Gulf Coast colonial period.
- Some transcriptions published in *Publications of the Mississippi Historical Society* and similar 19th-century compilations.

---

## Digitized / Online Access Summary

| Collection | Where | Coverage | Online? |
|------------|-------|----------|---------|
| 1800 U.S. Census (Washington Co.) | FamilySearch / Ancestry | 1800 | ✅ Indexed |
| 1810 U.S. Census | FamilySearch / Ancestry | 1810 | ✅ Indexed |
| BLM Land Patents | glorecords.blm.gov | 1800s+ | ✅ Searchable |
| Mobile Catholic Registers | FamilySearch (partial) | 1704+ | ⚠️ Partial |
| Alabama Territorial Records | FamilySearch | 1803+ sparse | ⚠️ Partial |
| Washington Co. Probate | ADAH / FamilySearch microfilm | 1800+ | ❌ Mostly undigitized |
| Spanish colonial records (AGI) | AGI Portal (pares.mcu.es) | pre-1813 | ⚠️ Partial — browse only |
| Mississippi Territory court records | MDAH | 1798–1817 | ❌ Physical only |

**Browsable (non-indexed) volumes on FamilySearch:** The agent found **none** for the pre-1820 Alabama window specifically. The AGI's PARES portal does provide some browsable digitized images of colonial records, but navigation requires knowing the specific *legajo* (bundle) reference.

---

## Recommended Research Path

1. **Identify the county** your ancestor was in — this determines which sovereign's records apply and which archive holds them.
2. **Start with the 1800 and 1810 censuses** — both are online and indexed.
3. **Check BLM GLO records** for land patents — often the earliest documentary trace.
4. **Write to ADAH** (adah.alabama.gov) for Washington or Madison County records not yet digitized.
5. For coastal ancestors: **contact the Archdiocese of Mobile** for baptism/marriage/burial registers and check FamilySearch's Mobile Catholic collection.
6. For Spanish-era research: the **PARES portal** (pares.mcu.es) provides browse access to AGI holdings; budget time to navigate by *legajo*.

---

*This guide covers Alabama as a whole. Individual county-level jurisdictions (Washington, Madison, Baldwin, Mobile) would each warrant their own more granular survey once you've narrowed to a specific family location.*

Here is the locality guide the subagent produced:

---

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1890)

*(Schuylkill County focus — with notes on the broader five-county region)*

## Jurisdiction Overview

**Core anthracite counties:** Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna (carved from Luzerne in 1878), Northumberland, and Carbon.

**Key boundary change:** Records for the Scranton/Carbondale area before 1878 fall under Luzerne County, not Lackawanna County.

**County seat (Schuylkill):** Pottsville | **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton

**Population (Schuylkill County):**
- 1860: 89,510 → 1870: 116,428 → 1880: 129,974

**Ethnic composition:** Large post-Famine Irish-born population (1847–1860s+), substantial Welsh and English miners, growing Eastern European communities from the 1880s.

**Key historical events:** Civil War (1861–1865); Molly Maguires trials centered on Pottsville (1876–1877); Great Railroad Strike of 1877.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records — CRITICAL GAP

> **Pennsylvania had no statewide birth or death registration until 1906.** For 1860–1890, there are no civil birth or death series. Church registers are the only vital substitute.

- **Marriage records (civil):** Available at county level:
  - *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950* — 312,045 records, indexed with images
  - *Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950* — 524,189 records, indexed with images
  - *Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900* — 198,765 records, index only
  - Schuylkill County marriage volume (DGS 007936753, 1870–1910, 94 images): **0% indexed — browse-only**
- **Death certificates:** *Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968* — useful for individuals who survived past 1906.

### Church Records

- **Primary for Irish families:** Roman Catholic
- **Diocese split by date:**
  - Parishes established **before 1868** → Diocese of Harrisburg archives
  - Parishes established **after 1868** → Diocese of Scranton archives
- A family arriving in the 1850s and staying into the 1870s may have records split across both dioceses.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records, 1708–1985* — 1,245,830 records, 982,415 persons, 607,220 images (indexed)
- **Browse-only volume:** DGS 007936751 (1842–1895, 187 images) — English and German; must be browsed image by image.

### Census Records

- **Federal censuses 1860, 1870, 1880:** Indexed and searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **1890 federal census: almost entirely destroyed by fire (1921).** No confirmed Schuylkill County fragments survive. Use triennial tax assessments, city directories, and church records as substitutes.
- **Mortality schedules (1860, 1870, 1880):** Record deaths in the preceding year — the closest substitute for missing death records. Check for every known death in those census years.
- **Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments (from 1853):** List householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity. Critical given the 1890 loss.

### Naturalization Records (Critical for Irish Men)

- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in **any court of record** — not just federal courts and not just the home county.
- **Schuylkill County volume:** DGS 007936750 (1849–1915, 298 images): **0% indexed — browse-only. Must be examined image by image.**
- NARA Mid-Atlantic Region (Philadelphia) holds federal-court naturalizations.

### Probate / Court Records

- *Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994* — 3,200,560 images, **0% indexed — browse-only.**
- Schuylkill County probate volume DGS 007936749 (1851–1930, 412 images): **0% indexed — browse-only.**
- Original records: Schuylkill County Register of Wills, Pottsville.

### Land / Deed Records

- Pennsylvania is a **metes-and-bounds state** — no federal rectangular-survey patents apply.
- **Practical note:** Many Irish miners lived in company-owned patch-town housing and never held real property. Prioritize tax lists and naturalization records over deed searches.
- Schuylkill County deed volume DGS 007936752 (1815–1900, 543 images): **22% indexed** — the most-indexed volume in the county holdings.

### Military Records

- Civil War: Service records and pension files at NARA (indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch); Pennsylvania State Archives holds adjutant general records.
- **Notable unit:** 48th Pennsylvania Infantry, recruited from coal miners, included many Irish men.
- **Molly Maguires trial records (1876–1877):** Carbon and Schuylkill County court records name dozens of Irish defendants and witnesses — not standard genealogical records but valuable for identifying families.

### Cemetery Records

- **FindAGrave and BillionGraves** have Schuylkill County coverage, but Catholic patch-town cemetery coverage is uneven.
- Sexton records and burial registers are held by individual parishes and diocesan archives.

### Newspapers

- ***Miners' Journal*** (Pottsville, founded 1825): Obituaries, marriage notices, court proceedings, mine-accident reports. **Mine accident reports often name the deceased miner, nationality, and surviving family — a critical substitute for missing death records.**
- Microfilm at the Schuylkill County Historical Society; partial digitization via GenealogyBank and Chronicling America (Library of Congress, free).

### Immigration Records

- Ports of entry: Philadelphia (closest), New York (Castle Garden, 1855–1890), Baltimore.
- Passenger arrival lists indexed on Ancestry, FamilySearch, and MyHeritage.
- **Irish civil registration (births, marriages, deaths from 1864)** and **Griffith's Valuation (1847–1864)** may document the Irish family of origin — see the FS Wiki page on [Ireland Emigration and Immigration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Emigration_and_Immigration).

---

## Specialized Coal-Region Indexes

*(From the FamilySearch Wiki: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))*

1. **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898:** Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the lower anthracite field, drawn from surviving company payroll books. Entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and **parish of origin where stated**. This data can directly identify an ancestor's Irish county of origin — check this before any other source for a male miner.

2. **Colliery payroll books vs. mine-inspection reports:** Payroll-derived indexes name individual workers; mine-inspection and accident reports are organized by colliery, not by person. Payroll indexes are the more direct finding aid for an individual.

3. **Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments (from 1853):** See Census section above; also a specialized finding aid noted in the wiki.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Schuylkill County Church Records 1708–1985 (1.2M records, indexed); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (indexed); Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906–1968 (indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal censuses 1860/1870/1880 (indexed); Pennsylvania Tax & Exoneration Lists 1768–1801 | Subscription |
| GenealogyBank | *Miners' Journal* digitized runs (partial) | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (LOC) | Newspaper digitization — check for *Miners' Journal* runs | Free |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deeds, wills, naturalization papers, court minutes, marriage licenses |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Triennial tax assessments, adjutant general records, mine inspection reports |
| Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville | *Miners' Journal* microfilm, county histories, cemetery surveys |
| Diocese of Harrisburg Archives | Catholic parish registers for pre-1868 parishes |
| Diocese of Scranton Archives | Catholic parish registers for post-1868 parishes |
| NARA Mid-Atlantic Region, Philadelphia | Federal naturalization records (post-1906), federal court records |
| Hagley Museum & Library, Wilmington DE | Philadelphia & Reading Railroad records, coal company records |

---

## Records NOT Online

- Civil birth and death records for 1860–1890 **do not exist as a civil series**.
- Triennial tax assessment ledgers for most of the coal region are **not digitized**.
- Mine inspector annual reports and mine accident books are physical, at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- Company store ledgers and most colliery payroll books are undigitized.
- Ancient Order of Hibernians (AOH) chapter records are in AOH custody, not online.
- Most Catholic parish registers for the coal region remain in diocesan archives, **not systematically online**.

---

## Key Research Warnings

1. **No birth or death registration 1860–1890** — church registers are the only vital source, and most are in physical diocesan custody.
2. **Nearly all digitized Schuylkill County volumes on FamilySearch are browse-only** — no name search, image-by-image examination required. The exception is the church records collection (indexed) and deed records (22% indexed).
3. **The 1890 census is gone.** Plan around it: triennial tax assessments, church registers, city directories, and the *Miners' Journal* fill the gap.
4. **Distinguish the two Catholic dioceses by date** (1868 split). A family may have records in both Harrisburg and Scranton archives.
5. **This guide covers Schuylkill County.** Luzerne, Lackawanna (records before 1878 under Luzerne), Northumberland, and Carbon each need a separate locality survey.

The locality entry has been saved to the project as `loc_001`.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1890)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:**
  - 1860: 89,510
  - 1870: 116,428
  - 1880: 129,974
  (US Census figures for Schuylkill County)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated; company-owned collieries employed the majority of adult males. The Reading Railroad was the dominant coal carrier.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish-born population from the post-Famine wave (1847–1860s onward), substantial Welsh and English miners, growing Eastern European (Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian) communities from the 1880s. Germans were present in older agricultural settlements.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish), Welsh Calvinist Methodist and Congregationalist, Anglican/Episcopalian, Lutheran and German Reformed (older German settlers), various Protestant denominations for Welsh and English miners.
- **Key historical events:** Opening of the anthracite fields (1820s–1840s); Civil War draft and enlistment (1861–1865); Molly Maguires trials (1876–1877, centered on Pottsville); Great Railroad Strike of 1877; labor organizing and mine safety legislation throughout the 1880s.

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County has been stable since its formation in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties.
- No significant boundary changes occurred during the 1860–1890 research window.
- The broader anthracite coal region spans five counties. Lackawanna County was carved from Luzerne County in 1878 — if researching the Scranton/Carbondale area, records before 1878 are under Luzerne County, not Lackawanna.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration of births or deaths until 1906 (state level). For 1860–1890 events, there is no statewide birth or death registration series to search.
- **What exists for 1860–1890:** County-level marriage registrations were recorded at county courthouses and are the only civil vital series broadly available for this period. FamilySearch holds:
  - *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950* (collection 1571957): 312,045 records, indexed
  - *Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950* (collection 1921317): 524,189 records, 1,048,378 persons, indexed — overlaps the end of this research window
  - *Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900* (collection 1502909): 198,765 compiled records, no images
  - One browse-only digitized volume of Schuylkill County marriage records (DGS 007936753, 1870–1910): 94 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image
- **Death certificates:** The *Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968* collection (2,255,317 records, fully indexed with images) covers deaths from 1906 onward — outside the 1860–1890 window but useful for tracing the later lives and deaths of individuals born in this period.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth registration series exists for 1860–1890. No civil death registration series exists for 1860–1890. Church registers are the primary substitute.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic baptismal registers, Protestant baptism/christening registers, cemetery records, mortality schedules of the federal census (1860, 1870, 1880).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (primary for Irish immigrants), Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Congregationalist, Anglican, Lutheran, German Reformed.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations (a separate dated event — check confirmation registers separately from baptismal registers).
- **Where held:**
  - Catholic parishes established before 1868: Diocese of Harrisburg archives
  - Catholic parishes established after 1868: Diocese of Scranton archives
  - Many coal-region Catholic parishes were founded 1840–1870 specifically to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities (per the *Pennsylvania Coal Region Records* wiki page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)
  - FamilySearch holds one digitized volume of Schuylkill County church records (DGS 007936751, 1842–1895, 187 images): **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Languages: English and German. Must be browsed image by image; researcher must read both languages.
  - FamilySearch collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (*Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records*, 1708–1985): 1,245,830 records, 982,415 persons, 607,220 images.
- **Language note:** Some records, particularly from German Reformed and Lutheran congregations, are in German. Irish Catholic records are in Latin (sacramental entries) with English marginalia.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Available for Schuylkill County for 1860, 1870, and 1880 (the years directly covering this research window). The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed by fire; only a fragment survives nationally.
- **Mortality schedules:** The federal census mortality schedules for 1860, 1870, and 1880 record deaths in the year preceding the census — a valuable substitute for missing death records.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not take a state census during this period.
- **Triennial tax assessments:** Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents triennially from 1853, listing householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity — these serve as intercensal substitutes and are particularly valuable given the 1890 census loss. See the *Pennsylvania Coal Region Records* wiki page.
- **Access:** Federal census years 1860, 1870, and 1880 are indexed and searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1850 Schuylkill County census is also available on Ancestry (collection 1276).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Date range:** From county formation (1811); the relevant window is 1860–1890.
- **Where held / digitization:**
  - FamilySearch collection 1999196 (*Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994*): 3,200,560 images, 0 indexed records — **browse-only images** with no name index. Must be browsed volume by volume.
  - Digitized volume DGS 007936749 (Schuylkill County Probate Records, 1851–1930, 412 images): **browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text searchable.
  - Original records held at the Schuylkill County Register of Wills, Pottsville.
- **Naturalization records:**
  - Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record (Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, Orphans' Court). Irish miners frequently naturalized shortly after arrival or before elections.
  - Digitized volume DGS 007936750 (Schuylkill County Naturalization Records, 1849–1915, 298 images): **browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image.
  - NARA Philadelphia holds federal-court naturalizations.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state — no federal rectangular-survey patents apply here).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania (via the General Land Office of Pennsylvania and predecessor proprietors) granted the land; deeds for subsequent transfers are filed at the county level.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records. Company-owned coal-patch housing means many miners never owned real property — search company records and tax lists as the primary land-equivalent evidence.
- **Where held / digitization:**

Church records in volume DGS 007936751 cover 1842-1895 and are in English and German — the researcher must read both languages. This volume is browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text searchable).
Naturalization records (volume DGS 007936750, 1849-1915) are browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image.

The anthracite coal region spans five counties: Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Carbon. Search all five if the exact county of residence is unknown. Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Carbon each need their own locality survey.

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1890)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:**
  - 1860: 89,510
  - 1870: 116,428
  - 1880: 129,974
  (US Census figures for Schuylkill County)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated; company-owned collieries employed the majority of adult males. The Reading Railroad was the dominant coal carrier.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish-born population from the post-Famine wave (1847–1860s onward), substantial Welsh and English miners, growing Eastern European (Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian) communities from the 1880s. Germans were present in older agricultural settlements.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish), Welsh Calvinist Methodist and Congregationalist, Anglican/Episcopalian, Lutheran and German Reformed (older German settlers), various Protestant denominations for Welsh and English miners.
- **Key historical events:** Opening of the anthracite fields (1820s–1840s); Civil War draft and enlistment (1861–1865); Molly Maguires trials (1876–1877, centered on Pottsville); Great Railroad Strike of 1877; labor organizing and mine safety legislation throughout the 1880s.

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County has been stable since its formation in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties.
- No significant boundary changes occurred during the 1860–1890 research window.
- The broader anthracite coal region spans five counties. Lackawanna County was carved from Luzerne County in 1878 — if researching the Scranton/Carbondale area, records before 1878 are under Luzerne County, not Lackawanna.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration of births or deaths until 1906 (state level). For 1860–1890 events, there is no statewide birth or death registration series to search.
- **What exists for 1860–1890:** County-level marriage registrations were recorded at county courthouses and are the only civil vital series broadly available for this period. FamilySearch holds:
  - *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950* (collection 1571957): 312,045 records, indexed
  - *Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950* (collection 1921317): 524,189 records, 1,048,378 persons, indexed — overlaps the end of this research window
  - *Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900* (collection 1502909): 198,765 compiled records, no images
  - One browse-only digitized volume of Schuylkill County marriage records (DGS 007936753, 1870–1910): 94 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image
- **Death certificates:** The *Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968* collection (2,255,317 records, fully indexed with images) covers deaths from 1906 onward — outside the 1860–1890 window but useful for tracing the later lives and deaths of individuals born in this period.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth registration series exists for 1860–1890. No civil death registration series exists for 1860–1890. Church registers are the primary substitute.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic baptismal registers, Protestant baptism/christening registers, cemetery records, mortality schedules of the federal census (1860, 1870, 1880).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (primary for Irish immigrants), Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Congregationalist, Anglican, Lutheran, German Reformed.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations (a separate dated event — check confirmation registers separately from baptismal registers).
- **Where held:**
  - Catholic parishes established before 1868: Diocese of Harrisburg archives
  - Catholic parishes established after 1868: Diocese of Scranton archives
  - Many coal-region Catholic parishes were founded 1840–1870 specifically to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities (per the *Pennsylvania Coal Region Records* wiki page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)
  - FamilySearch holds one digitized volume of Schuylkill County church records (DGS 007936751, 1842–1895, 187 images): **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Languages: English and German. Must be browsed image by image; researcher must read both languages.
  - FamilySearch collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (*Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records*, 1708–1985): 1,245,830 records, 982,415 persons, 607,220 images.
- **Language note:** Some records, particularly from German Reformed and Lutheran congregations, are in German. Irish Catholic records are in Latin (sacramental entries) with English marginalia.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Available for Schuylkill County for 1860, 1870, and 1880 (the years directly covering this research window). The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed by fire; only a fragment survives nationally.
- **Mortality schedules:** The federal census mortality schedules for 1860, 1870, and 1880 record deaths in the year preceding the census — a valuable substitute for missing death records.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not take a state census during this period.
- **Triennial tax assessments:** Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents triennially from 1853, listing householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity — these serve as intercensal substitutes and are particularly valuable given the 1890 census loss. See the *Pennsylvania Coal Region Records* wiki page.
- **Access:** Federal census years 1860, 1870, and 1880 are indexed and searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1850 Schuylkill County census is also available on Ancestry (collection 1276).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Date range:** From county formation (1811); the relevant window is 1860–1890.
- **Where held / digitization:**
  - FamilySearch collection 1999196 (*Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994*): 3,200,560 images, 0 indexed records — **browse-only images** with no name index. Must be browsed volume by volume.
  - Digitized volume DGS 007936749 (Schuylkill County Probate Records, 1851–1930, 412 images): **browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text searchable.
  - Original records held at the Schuylkill County Register of Wills, Pottsville.
- **Naturalization records:**
  - Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record (Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, Orphans' Court). Irish miners frequently naturalized shortly after arrival or before elections.
  - Digitized volume DGS 007936750 (Schuylkill County Naturalization Records, 1849–1915, 298 images): **browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image.
  - NARA Philadelphia holds federal-court naturalizations.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state — no federal rectangular-survey patents apply here).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania (via the General Land Office of Pennsylvania and predecessor proprietors) granted the land; deeds for subsequent transfers are filed at the county level.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records. Company-owned coal-patch housing means many miners never owned real property — search company records and tax lists as the primary land-equivalent evidence.
- **Where held / digitization:**
  - Digitized volume DGS 007936752 (Schuylkill County Deed Records, 1815–1900, 543 images): **partially indexed** — 22% name-indexed; images available. This is the highest-indexed volume in the Schuylkill County holdings.
  - Original deeds held at the Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — Schuylkill County furnished substantial infantry and cavalry regiments. Irish miners were prominent in units such as the 48th Pennsylvania Infantry (coal miners' regiment).
- **Record types:** Civil War service records and pension files at NARA (indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch); Pennsylvania State Archives holds state-level adjutant general records; draft registration records at NARA.
- **Molly Maguires trial records (1876–1877):** Court records from the Carbon and Schuylkill County trials name Irish defendants and witnesses — held at the respective county courthouses and in published contemporary accounts. Not genealogical records in the standard sense, but they name dozens of Irish families.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Numerous Catholic parish cemeteries (St. Patrick's Pottsville and other Irish parishes), independent miners' cemeteries, Welsh chapel burial grounds.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves have coverage for Schuylkill County cemeteries, though coverage for Catholic patch-town cemeteries is uneven.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held by individual parishes and cemetery associations. Diocesan archives (Harrisburg pre-1868, Scranton post-1868) may hold copies.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The *Miners' Journal* (Pottsville, founded 1825) is the flagship coal-region paper and ran throughout the entire 1860–1890 window. It carried obituaries, marriage notices, court proceedings, accident reports, and labor news. The *Pottsville Evening Chronicle* and other county papers also ran during portions of this period.
- **Where held:** The *Miners' Journal* is on microfilm at the Schuylkill County Historical Society and partially digitized through various newspaper archives. Chronicling America (Library of Congress) and GenealogyBank should be checked for digitized runs.
- **Content value:** Mine accident reports in the *Miners' Journal* often name the deceased miner, their nationality, and surviving family — a critical substitute for missing death records.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Context:** Irish immigrants to the coal region arrived predominantly via Philadelphia, New York, or Baltimore. Chain migration from specific Irish counties (Donegal, Mayo, Galway, Cork) was common.
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia (closest major port to Schuylkill County), New York (Castle Garden, 1855–1890), Baltimore.
- **Record types:**
  - Passenger arrival lists at NARA (indexed on Ancestry, FamilySearch, and MyHeritage for this period)
  - Pre-1906 naturalization declarations and petitions at county courts (Schuylkill County, volume DGS 007936750)
  - The *Ireland Emigration and Immigration* wiki page was returned only as a generic records page — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Emigration_and_Immigration directly
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.
- **Reverse emigration:** Some miners returned to Ireland periodically or sent remittances — Irish civil registration (births, marriages, deaths from 1864) and Griffith's Valuation (1847–1864) may document the family of origin.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania triennial state assessments (from 1853); county property tax records.
- **Date range:** Triennial assessments run from 1853 through the entire research window.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds assessment ledgers; some are on FamilySearch microfilm.
- **Substitute value:** Triennial assessments are the primary intercensal substitute given the 1890 federal census loss. They list householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity — directly relevant to identifying Irish miners.
- **Ancestry collection:** *Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801* (Ancestry collection 7667) predates the research window but is available as context for established families.

### Specialized coal-region indexes
The FamilySearch Wiki page *Pennsylvania Coal Region Records* (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) identifies three sources unique to the anthracite field:

1. **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898:** Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated. This is a specialized finding aid not available through standard FamilySearch collection search.
2. **Colliery payroll books vs. mine-inspection reports:** The wiki distinguishes company payroll indexes (which name individual workers) from mine-inspection and accident reports (organized by colliery, not by person). For an individual Irish miner, payroll-derived indexes are the more direct finding aid, especially where census indexing was inconsistent.
3. **Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments from 1853:** Assessment ledgers list householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity — particularly valuable as census substitutes.

### Other record types
- **Company/occupational records:** Mining companies (Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company, Lehigh Coal and Navigation, etc.) maintained employment records, accident books, and company store ledgers. Survival is scattered; the Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies hold some. The Hagley Museum and Library (Wilmington, DE) holds Philadelphia and Reading Railroad records.
- **Fraternal and mutual-aid records:** The Ancient Order of Hibernians (AOH) was active in the coal region; chapter records name Irish members and may document deaths, illness benefits, and family relationships. Contact the AOH national archives.
- **Mine-accident reports:** Pennsylvania Mine Inspector reports (published annually from 1870) list mine accidents by colliery and sometimes name victims. Available at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **School records:** Township and borough school enrollment records are held locally and are uneven in survival.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Schuylkill County Church Records (1708–1985, 1.2M records); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312K records); Pennsylvania County Marriages 1885–1950 (524K records); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (199K records); Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906–1968 (4.2M records) | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850 Schuylkill County Federal Census (collection 1276); Pennsylvania Tax and Exoneration Lists 1768–1801 (collection 7667); federal census years 1860, 1870, 1880 (national collections) | Subscription |
| GenealogyBank | Miners' Journal digitized runs (partial) | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (LOC) | Newspaper digitization — check for Miners' Journal runs | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 5 digitized volumes for Schuylkill County, and totalResults = 5, so this is the complete set. All five are detailed above. None of the volumes targeting 1860–1890 vital events is name-indexed; the highest-indexed volume is deed records at 22%.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Original deeds, wills, naturalization papers, court minutes, marriage licenses | In-person or mail request |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Triennial tax assessments, adjutant general records, state agency records | In-person; some online via PA State Archives portal |
| Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville | Miners' Journal microfilm, county histories, cemetery surveys, local photographs | In-person; limited mail service |
| Diocese of Harrisburg Archives | Catholic parish registers for pre-1868 parishes | Contact diocesan archivist |
| Diocese of Scranton Archives | Catholic parish registers for post-1868 parishes | Contact diocesan archivist |
| NARA Mid-Atlantic Region, Philadelphia | Federal naturalization records (post-1906), federal court records | In-person or online request |
| Hagley Museum and Library, Wilmington DE | Philadelphia and Reading Railroad records, coal company records | In-person; finding aids online |

## Records NOT online
- Civil birth and death records for 1860–1890 do not exist as a civil series (statewide registration began 1906) — church registers are the only vital source and most remain in diocesan or parish custody, not online.
- Triennial tax assessment ledgers for most of the coal region are not digitized or indexed online.
- Mine-accident reports and mine inspector annual reports are in physical form at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- Company store ledgers, colliery payroll books (except those captured in the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index), and employment records are largely undigitized, held by the Pennsylvania State Archives and Hagley Museum.
- Ancient Order of Hibernians chapter records are in AOH custody and not online.
- Most Catholic parish registers for the coal region are held in diocesan archives and are not systematically online.

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed by fire (1921) — only fragments survive nationally, none confirmed for Schuylkill County. Use triennial tax assessments, city/borough directories, and church registers as substitutes.
- No major courthouse fire is documented for Schuylkill County (unlike many Pennsylvania counties), so the pre-1890 county records baseline is relatively intact.
- Company records lost in the 1903 records consolidation: the *Pennsylvania Coal Region Records* wiki notes that surviving payroll books from before the consolidation are what underpins the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index — many other company books did not survive.

## Research tips
- **Start with the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** for any male ancestor who worked in the lower anthracite field 1855–1898. Its parish-of-origin field, where filled in, can short-circuit the search for Irish county of origin. See https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records
- **Distinguish the two Catholic dioceses by date:** Pre-1868 parish registers are under Harrisburg; post-1868 under Scranton. An Irish family arriving in the 1850s and staying into the 1870s may have records in both dioceses.
- **Use the Miners' Journal as a primary source.** Mine accident reports, court proceedings (especially Molly Maguires-era 1876–1877), and obituaries appeared regularly and name Irish individuals whose vital records are otherwise absent.
- **Naturalization timeline matters for Irish men:** An Irishman who arrived in the 1850s would have filed a declaration of intention and petition in a Pennsylvania court of record — any county court, not just federal. Search Schuylkill County Quarter Sessions court minutes (browse-only, DGS 007936750) and also neighboring county courts if the man moved.
- **Pennsylvania is a metes-and-bounds state** — there are no federal patent records for land here. However, many Irish miners in company-owned patches never held title; focus on tax lists and naturalization records rather than deed records for tracking movement.
- **Search adjoining counties.** Neighboring counties (Berks, Lebanon, Northumberland, Columbia, Luzerne, Carbon) share borders with Schuylkill. A family living near a county line generated records on both sides. The neighboring county table from the Schuylkill County Genealogy wiki page was not returned (the page returned generic content), so treat all six adjoining counties as potential research targets.
- **The five anthracite counties are not interchangeable.** Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Carbon each have their own record holdings, court jurisdictions, and Catholic diocesan affiliations. Each needs its own locality survey before systematic research begins.
- **Mortality schedules** (1860, 1870, 1880 federal census) record deaths in the preceding year and are the closest substitute for civil death records in this period — check them for every known death in those census years.
